title: Physiotherapy for Arthritis — How It Helps and How to Access It
excerpt: Everything you need to know about physiotherapy for arthritis: what it involves, NHS self-referral, private costs, hydrotherapy, and exercises you can do at home.
content:
Clinically reviewed by Louis Maxwell, First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483. Last updated: June 2026.

Quick answer: Physiotherapy helps arthritis by providing a comprehensive assessment, exercise programmes, and manual therapy. Physiotherapists offer pain management advice, joint protection techniques, and gait re-training. You can access physiotherapy on the NHS via GP referral or self-referral, or privately. Your first appointment includes assessment, physical examination, and a personalised treatment plan.

If there is one healthcare professional every person with arthritis should know about, it is a physiotherapist. Physiotherapy is a cornerstone of arthritis treatment — recommended by NICE as a first-line approach for osteoarthritis, and a vital part of the multidisciplinary care recommended for rheumatoid arthritis. This guide explains exactly what physio can do for your joints, how to access it on the NHS, what private treatment costs, and what to expect at your first appointment.

What Can a Physiotherapist Do for Arthritis?

A physiotherapist is a movement and rehabilitation expert. They do far more than hand you a sheet of exercises. Their role includes: comprehensive assessment (looking at your whole body — how you walk, sit, stand, what muscles are weak or tight), exercise prescription (a personalised programme for your body, your joints, and your goals), manual therapy (hands-on techniques to mobilise stiff joints and release tight muscles), pain management advice (education on pacing, flare management, and using movement to reduce pain), joint protection techniques (teaching you how to move in ways that reduce strain on damaged joints), gait re-training (improving how you walk to reduce joint stress), and referral and liaison (connecting you with occupational therapy, orthopaedics, pain management programmes). UK physiotherapists are regulated by the Health and Care Professions Council (HCPC) and are often members of the Chartered Society of Physiotherapy (CSP). You are in safe hands.

Types of Physiotherapy for Arthritis

Exercise-based physiotherapy is the bread and butter of arthritis care — your physio designs a programme of strengthening, flexibility, and balance exercises tailored to your joints and fitness level. Manual therapy involves hands-on joint mobilisation (gentle, controlled movements) and soft-tissue massage — providing short-term relief and helping you move more freely. Some NHS physiotherapists are trained in acupuncture — evidence for arthritis is mixed but some people find it helps. Electrotherapy (ultrasound, laser) is sometimes used though the evidence base is limited. Perhaps most importantly, education and self-management — your physio teaches you about your condition and gives you tools to manage it yourself, for life.

How to Get Physiotherapy on the NHS

There are two main routes. Route 1 — GP referral: your GP refers you to your local NHS physiotherapy service. The physiotherapy department contacts you with an appointment. Route 2 — NHS MSK self-referral: in many parts of the UK, you can refer yourself directly to an NHS musculoskeletal (MSK) physiotherapy service — no GP appointment needed. This is faster and takes pressure off GP surgeries.

NHS MSK Self-Referral — How It Works

Self-referral (also called "self-refer" or "direct access") is available in many areas of England, Scotland, and Wales. Here is how: 1) Find your local service — search online for "NHS physiotherapy self-referral [your area]" or check your GP practice website. 2) Complete a form — usually online but sometimes by phone — answering questions about your symptoms, general health, and what you need help with. 3) Triage — a physiotherapist reviews your form and decides if physiotherapy is appropriate and how quickly you need to be seen. 4) Appointment — if accepted, you receive an appointment, usually within a few weeks. Most adults with muscle or joint problems can self-refer. NHS physiotherapy is free at the point of use.

Private Physiotherapy — Costs and What to Expect

If NHS waiting times are long in your area or you want more frequent sessions, private physiotherapy is an option. Initial assessment costs £45–£80 and follow-up sessions cost £40–£65. Many clinics offer packages (e.g., 6 sessions for a reduced rate). Some health insurance policies cover physiotherapy. Look for HCPC registration (mandatory) and CSP membership with specialist interests (e.g., arthritis, rheumatology). The CSP "Physio2U" directory and "Physio First" network are good places to search. Private sessions usually offer longer appointments (45–60 minutes vs 20–30 minutes on NHS), more flexibility on appointment times (evenings, weekends), and continuity (same physio every time).

Hydrotherapy for Arthritis

Hydrotherapy (aquatic physiotherapy) is performed in a warm-water pool (usually 33–36°C) with a physiotherapist guiding specific exercises. It is not just swimming. The water's buoyancy supports body weight, reducing stress on joints. The warmth relaxes muscles and eases stiffness. Moving through water strengthens muscles gently. Hydrotherapy is ideal if land-based exercise is too painful. Research shows it reduces pain and improves function in both OA and RA. It is available on the NHS in some areas (usually hospital physiotherapy departments), though access varies. Private hydrotherapy sessions cost £50–£80.

What to Expect at Your First Physio Appointment

Before you go: wear loose comfortable clothing, bring a list of your medications, and think about your goals (what would you like to be able to do that you cannot do now?). During the appointment (45–60 minutes): conversation about your pain, general health, work, hobbies, and what matters to you; physical assessment — you may be asked to walk, sit, stand, and perform simple movements — the physio may gently feel your joints and test strength and range of motion (you can stop at any time); explanation of findings; and together you agree on a treatment plan — exercises, goals, and follow-up appointments. After: you will usually leave with 2–4 exercises to practise. Consistency is everything. Follow-up sessions every 2–4 weeks to check progress.

In many areas you can ask your local integrated care board about self-referral to physiotherapy or lifestyle support without waiting for a hospital letter. Check your GP surgery website or the NHS App for the route that applies where you live.

Working with NHS pathways

Most people start with GP care, community physiotherapy and self-management, with rheumatology involved when inflammatory disease is suspected or treatment needs escalate. Ask what monitoring blood tests or reviews you should expect, and who to contact between appointments if a flare escalates.

Preparing for appointments

Write three priorities before you go: main symptom, functional limit (stairs, sleep, work), and the question you most need answered. Bring a current medicine list including over-the-counter products. If English is not your first language, request an interpreter when you book.

Quick questions about Physiotherapy Arthritis Helps Access

Is this a substitute for seeing a clinician? No. Use it to prepare questions and understand options, then confirm decisions with your NHS team.

How long before I judge whether a change helped? Give most habit or exercise changes at least two to four weeks, unless pain or swelling clearly worsens — in that case scale back sooner.

What should I track? Joint pain (0–10), morning stiffness time, sleep quality, and how far you can walk or how long you can type or stand. Patterns beat one-off ratings.

Safety and when to get urgent help

This page is general information for people in the United Kingdom, not personal medical advice. Seek urgent help via NHS 111 or A&E if you have sudden inability to move a joint, hot swollen joint with fever, chest pain, severe shortness of breath, or symptoms that feel immediately dangerous.

title: Arthritis Pain Management — A Kind, Practical Guide
excerpt: Manage arthritis pain with a whole-person UK approach: movement, heat and cold, medication, mindfulness, sleep, complementary therapies and emotional support.
content:
Clinically reviewed by Louis Maxwell, First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483. Last updated: June 2026.

Quick answer: Arthritis pain is influenced by physical factors, muscle tension, nervous system sensitisation, emotions, and sleep. Effective management takes a whole-person approach: exercise, sensible medication use, heat and cold therapy, and mindfulness. Prioritising sleep, setting realistic daily goals, and having a plan for flare-ups reduces pain and improves well-being. If pain affects your mood, speak to your GP.

Pain is the thing people most fear about arthritis. It can steal your sleep, sap your energy, and shrink your world. But pain is not simply something you must endure. It can be understood, managed, and — for many people — significantly reduced. This guide takes a whole-person approach. Pain is not just about joints. It is affected by how you move, eat, sleep, think, and feel. The more tools you have, the more control you gain.

Understanding Arthritis Pain

Arthritis pain is not a simple signal from a damaged joint to your brain. It is shaped by many factors: physical damage (cartilage loss, inflammation, joint changes), muscle tension (when joints hurt, surrounding muscles tighten protectively — causing more pain), sensitisation (over time the nervous system can become "tuned up" making pain feel worse than the physical damage alone would suggest), emotions and stress (anxiety, low mood, and stress lower pain tolerance and amplify pain), and fatigue and poor sleep (pain and sleep are locked in a miserable dance — pain disrupts sleep, and poor sleep makes pain worse). Managing pain effectively requires addressing more than just the joint.

Movement and Exercise for Pain Relief

It is the oldest paradox in arthritis: movement hurts, but not moving hurts more. Every NICE guideline on arthritis places exercise at the centre of pain management. Why it works: strengthening muscles reduces load on joints; movement stimulates synovial fluid release lubricating joints; exercise triggers endorphins — your body's natural painkillers; regular movement "calms down" a sensitised nervous system over time. What kind? Walking (start with 5–10 minutes), swimming or pool-based exercise, cycling, yoga or tai chi, physio-prescribed strength exercises. The key is pacing. A little every day beats a lot once a week.

Heat and Cold Therapy

Simple, cheap, and genuinely effective. Heat therapy is best for stiff, achy chronic pain (especially OA-related) — it relaxes muscles, improves blood flow, and eases stiffness. Try a warm bath or shower, a microwavable wheat bag, an electric heat pad (low setting, never sleep with it on), or warm water exercises. Cold therapy is best for hot, swollen, inflamed joints (common in RA, gout, or acute OA flares) — it numbs the area and reduces swelling. Try a bag of frozen peas wrapped in a tea towel (15 minutes max), a gel ice pack (never directly on skin), or a bowl of cool water for hands or feet. Some people find alternating heat and cold helpful.

Pain Medications — What Works

Medication is one tool among many. Paracetamol for mild-to-moderate pain (over the counter). NSAIDs (ibuprofen, naproxen) for pain plus inflammation (over the counter or prescription). Topical gels for localised joint pain (over the counter). Opioids (codeine, tramadol) for severe short-term pain (prescription only). DMARDs/biologics for underlying inflammation in RA (prescription, specialist). Steroid injections for flare-ups in a single joint (GP or rheumatologist). Always take medication at the dose prescribed and speak to your GP before making changes.

Mindfulness and Relaxation Techniques

It might sound "soft" compared to medication or surgery — but mindfulness and relaxation have solid evidence for reducing chronic pain. A 2019 review in the British Journal of Pain found mindfulness-based interventions reduced pain intensity and improved quality of life. Why it helps: reduces muscle tension, lowers stress hormones that amplify pain, changes your relationship with pain — making it feel less overwhelming. Simple techniques: box breathing (in for 4, hold for 4, out for 4, hold for 4 — repeat 5 times), body scan (lie down and mentally scan from toes to head noticing and releasing tension), guided relaxation apps (NHS-recommended like Headspace and Calm offer free sessions), progressive muscle relaxation (tense each muscle group for 5 seconds then release — work from feet to face).

Sleep and Pain — Breaking the Cycle

Pain makes sleep hard. Poor sleep makes pain worse. Breaking this cycle is one of the most impactful things you can do. Stick to a schedule — same bedtime and wake time every day. Create a wind-down ritual: a warm bath, a book (not a screen), gentle stretches, a heat pack. Manage your sleep environment: a supportive mattress, a pillow between your knees for hip or knee pain, cool room temperature. Avoid caffeine after 2pm and alcohol close to bedtime. If you wake in pain, have a plan — a wheat bag by the bed, medication within reach, a guided breathing exercise queued on your phone. If sleep problems persist, speak to your GP.

Complementary Approaches

Some approaches with reasonable evidence: acupuncture (NICE does not recommend it for OA on the NHS, but some people report meaningful relief — private sessions cost £40–£80), massage therapy (may ease muscle tension around painful joints), TENS (a small device delivering mild electrical pulses — NICE does not recommend for OA but some find it helpful, units cost £20–£50), capsaicin cream (from chilli peppers, applied to skin over a joint — takes 1–2 weeks of regular use to work).

Creating Your Pain Management Toolkit

Daily tools: gentle movement, heat pack during your morning coffee, anti-inflammatory food choices, mindfulness practice. Bad-day tools: pain medication as prescribed, ice or heat as needed, pacing — do one important thing then rest, distraction — a film, a friend, a book. Emergency tools (severe flare): GP or rheumatologist contact details, flare plan (medications, rest strategy), support network — someone to help with shopping, children, or pets.

When Pain Affects Your Mood — Getting Support

Living with persistent pain changes how you feel. It is not a sign of weakness to struggle. Anxiety and depression are more common in people with arthritis than in the general population. The NHS takes this seriously. Talk to your GP — they can refer you to NHS talking therapies (IAPT). These are free and effective. Join a support group — Arthritis Action and Versus Arthritis run groups across the UK, in person and online. Be honest with loved ones — hiding how you feel makes it harder for people to support you. Pain is not your fault. And you do not have to manage it alone.

Work, rights and practical adjustments

Under the Equality Act 2010, employers in Great Britain should consider reasonable adjustments when arthritis has a substantial long-term effect. That can mean flexible hours, more breaks, seating, parking closer to the entrance, or software that reduces typing strain. Acas and Citizens Advice both publish plain-English guides you can take into a meeting.

title: Anti-Inflammatory Diet for Arthritis — What to Eat for Happier Joints
excerpt: Discover the best anti-inflammatory foods for arthritis, a sample 3-day Mediterranean-style meal plan, foods to avoid, and joint-friendly supplements.
content:
Clinically reviewed by Louis Maxwell, First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483. Last updated: June 2026.

Quick answer: Diet does not cure arthritis, but a consistent anti-inflammatory pattern can reduce background inflammation, support joint health and improve wellbeing. The evidence points to a Mediterranean-style approach: more oily fish, vegetables, wholegrains, olive oil, nuts and berries; less red and processed meat, refined sugar and ultra-processed food. This guide is based on published research and NHS dietary advice.

Can what you eat really make a difference to your arthritis? The honest answer is yes — but not in the way the internet often promises. There is no "miracle food" that cures arthritis. What the evidence does show is that a consistent, balanced, anti-inflammatory way of eating can help reduce background inflammation, support joint health, and improve overall wellbeing. This guide is based on published research and NHS dietary advice — not fads.

How Diet Affects Arthritis Inflammation

Inflammation is your body's natural defence response. In rheumatoid arthritis, the immune system drives inflammation that attacks the joints. In osteoarthritis, inflammation plays a smaller but still meaningful role in pain and tissue damage. Certain foods contain compounds that can either promote or calm inflammation: highly processed items, refined sugars, unhealthy fats, and excess red meat can increase inflammatory markers, while fruits, vegetables, whole grains, oily fish, nuts, and olive oil contain antioxidants and healthy fats that help reduce inflammation. Diet is not a replacement for medication — especially in RA. But it is a powerful tool to use alongside your treatment plan.

The Mediterranean Diet and Arthritis (Evidence Summary)

If there is one diet for which the science is strongest, it is the Mediterranean diet. This is not a strict "diet" in the slimming sense — it is a traditional way of eating common in countries like Greece, Italy, and Spain. A 2018 review published in Rheumatology International found that following a Mediterranean diet reduced pain and improved physical function in people with osteoarthritis. Studies in rheumatoid arthritis have shown it may reduce disease activity and inflammatory markers. The diet is rich in polyphenols (plant compounds with antioxidant effects), omega-3 fatty acids, and fibre. It includes plenty of vegetables and fruit, whole grains, legumes, oily fish (at least twice a week), olive oil as the main cooking fat, nuts and seeds, and limited red meat, processed foods, and sugary items.

Top 15 Anti-Inflammatory Foods

  1. Oily fish (salmon, mackerel, sardines, herring) — Rich in omega-3 fatty acids proven to reduce inflammation.
  2. Extra virgin olive oil — Contains oleocanthal, a compound with effects similar to ibuprofen (though much milder).
  3. Broccoli — Packed with sulforaphane, an antioxidant that may slow cartilage damage.
  4. Spinach and leafy greens — High in vitamin E and other antioxidants.
  5. Berries (blueberries, strawberries, raspberries) — Rich in anthocyanins that reduce inflammatory markers.
  6. Cherries — Particularly tart cherries, shown to reduce gout attacks and inflammatory markers.
  7. Turmeric — Contains curcumin, a powerful anti-inflammatory. Combine with black pepper to boost absorption.
  8. Ginger — Shown in studies to reduce pain and inflammation in osteoarthritis.
  9. Garlic — Contains diallyl disulphide, which may limit pro-inflammatory proteins.
  10. Walnuts — High in omega-3 (ALA type) and antioxidants.
  11. Flaxseeds — Good plant source of omega-3.
  12. Green tea — Rich in polyphenols and antioxidants.
  13. Whole grains (oats, brown rice, quinoa) — Fibre helps reduce C-reactive protein (CRP), an inflammatory marker.
  14. Beans and lentils — High in fibre and antioxidants; excellent protein source reducing reliance on red meat.
  15. Dark chocolate (70%+ cocoa) — Contains flavonoids with anti-inflammatory properties. A small square — not the whole bar.

Foods That May Worsen Inflammation

No food needs to be banned forever. But reducing these may help: highly processed foods (crisps, biscuits, ready meals), sugary drinks and sweets, refined carbohydrates (white bread, white pasta, pastries), red and processed meats (burgers, sausages, bacon), fried foods, excess alcohol (no more than 14 units per week), and omega-6-heavy oils (corn, sunflower, soybean) used in processed foods — these may promote inflammation when not balanced by omega-3.

A Sample 3-Day Anti-Inflammatory Meal Plan

Day 1: Breakfast — porridge with oats, semi-skimmed milk, blueberries, and walnuts. Lunch — wholemeal pitta with hummus, cherry tomatoes, and spinach, plus an apple. Dinner — grilled salmon with roasted Mediterranean vegetables drizzled with olive oil, with brown rice. Snack — a small handful of almonds.

Day 2: Breakfast — Greek yoghurt with strawberries, flaxseeds, and a drizzle of honey. Lunch — lentil soup with wholemeal bread. Dinner — chicken and vegetable stir-fry with ginger, garlic, and turmeric, served with quinoa. Snack — a square of dark chocolate (70%+).

Day 3: Breakfast — scrambled eggs on wholemeal toast with grilled tomatoes, plus green tea. Lunch — mixed bean salad with olive oil and lemon dressing, plus rocket. Dinner — mackerel fillets with steamed broccoli and sweet potato wedges baked in olive oil. Snack — cherry tomatoes or carrot sticks.

Supplements That Support Joint Health

Food first — supplements second. Omega-3 (fish oil) has strong evidence for reducing inflammation in RA. Vitamin D is important for bone health — the NHS recommends everyone in the UK consider a 10mcg vitamin D supplement in autumn and winter. Glucosamine and chondroitin have mixed evidence — NICE does not recommend them on the NHS but they are available over the counter. Turmeric/curcumin has growing evidence for OA pain relief — look for formulations with enhanced absorption. Always speak to your GP or pharmacist before starting supplements — some interact with prescription medications.

Practical Tips for Changing Your Diet

  1. Start small. Change one meal at a time. Swap white bread for wholemeal. Add one extra vegetable portion today.
  2. Cook from scratch where you can. This automatically reduces processed ingredients.
  3. Batch cook. Make a big lentil soup or vegetable curry on Sunday and freeze portions for busy days.
  4. Use frozen fruit and vegetables. Just as nutritious as fresh, cheaper, and always available.
  5. Read labels. If you cannot pronounce most ingredients, it is probably ultra-processed.
  6. Don't aim for perfection. An anti-inflammatory diet is about what you eat most of the time — not every single meal.

Everyday eating patterns

No single food cures arthritis. Patterns rich in vegetables, fruit, pulses, wholegrains and oily fish are the ones most often discussed in UK dietetic advice for inflammatory conditions. Keep changes realistic: swap one ultra-processed snack for fruit and nuts, or cook with olive oil more often than seed oils marketed as miracle cures.

Building a joint-friendly routine

Start with short sessions you can repeat on most days. Warm water, cycling, or paced walking often suits stiff joints better than sudden high-impact bursts. Increase time or resistance slowly, and leave a rest day when a joint is hot, swollen or unusually painful. If you are unsure where to begin, ask about NHS physiotherapy or an exercise referral scheme via your GP surgery.

title: Osteoarthritis vs Rheumatoid Arthritis — Understanding the Differences
excerpt: Confused about OA and RA? Learn the key differences between osteoarthritis and rheumatoid arthritis in symptoms, causes, treatments, and diagnosis.
content:
Clinically reviewed by Louis Maxwell, First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483. Last updated: June 2026.

Quick answer: Osteoarthritis (OA) and rheumatoid arthritis (RA) both cause joint pain but differ fundamentally. OA involves cartilage breakdown, usually from wear and tear, and commonly affects knees, hips, and hands. RA is an autoimmune disease where the immune system attacks joint linings, causing inflammation and damage — typically symmetrical, often starting in smaller joints on both sides of the body.

"Arthritis" is an umbrella term. It covers more than 100 different conditions affecting the joints — but two types dominate the conversation: osteoarthritis (OA) and rheumatoid arthritis (RA). They share a name. They both cause joint pain. But they are very different diseases with different causes, different treatments, and different outcomes. Understanding which one you have matters enormously — because the right treatment depends on it.

What Is Osteoarthritis (OA)?

Osteoarthritis is the most common type of arthritis in the UK, affecting around 8.75 million people. It is sometimes called "wear-and-tear" arthritis, though that phrase oversimplifies things. The smooth cartilage that cushions the ends of your bones gradually breaks down. Over time, the joint space narrows, bone rubs on bone, and the joint itself may change shape. Small bony growths called osteophytes (bone spurs) may form. Commonly affected joints include knees, hips, hands (especially the ends of the fingers and base of the thumb), and the spine. OA becomes more common with age — most people are over 45 at diagnosis. Being overweight, having a previous joint injury, or a family history of OA all increase the risk. Pain typically worsens with activity and improves with rest. Morning stiffness usually lasts less than 30 minutes.

What Is Rheumatoid Arthritis (RA)?

Rheumatoid arthritis is an autoimmune disease. The body's immune system — which normally fights infection — mistakenly attacks the lining of the joints (the synovium). This causes inflammation, swelling, and eventually joint damage. RA affects around 430,000 people in the UK. It is less common than OA but generally more aggressive. The synovium becomes inflamed and thickened. Over time, this inflammation can erode cartilage and bone, leading to joint deformity. RA can also affect other parts of the body — the heart, lungs, eyes, and blood vessels. RA usually affects both sides of the body symmetrically — both hands, both wrists, both feet. Small joints are often affected first. It can start at any age, but most commonly begins between 40 and 60. Women are two to three times more likely to develop RA than men. Smoking is a major risk factor. Morning stiffness in RA often lasts more than an hour. Joints may feel hot, swollen, and tender. Fatigue and a general feeling of being unwell are common.

Key Differences at a Glance

  • What is it? OA is wear-and-repair breakdown of cartilage. RA is an autoimmune disease — the immune system attacks joints.
  • Who gets it? OA: more common with age (45+), linked to wear, injury, and weight. RA: can start at any age, women affected more, linked to genetics and smoking.
  • Joints affected: OA often one-sided — knees, hips, hands, spine. RA usually symmetrical (both sides) — hands, wrists, feet first.
  • Morning stiffness: OA — less than 30 minutes. RA — more than 1 hour.
  • Swelling: OA — bony, firm. RA — soft, warm, spongy.
  • Systemic symptoms: OA — rare. RA — common (fatigue, fever, weight loss, inflammation in other organs).
  • Blood tests: OA — normal inflammatory markers. RA — raised CRP/ESR; positive rheumatoid factor or anti-CCP antibodies in many cases.
  • Treatment focus: OA — exercise, weight management, pain relief, surgery if needed. RA — DMARDs, biologics, steroids to control the immune system.

Treatment Differences

OA treatment aims to manage symptoms and maintain function. NICE guidelines recommend a stepped approach: exercise and weight management first, then pain relief (paracetamol, NSAIDs), physiotherapy, joint injections (corticosteroids), and surgery (joint replacement). There are currently no drugs that slow OA progression. RA treatment aims to stop the immune system from attacking the joints and prevent permanent damage. Early, aggressive treatment is critical. The approach includes DMARDs (methotrexate usually first), corticosteroids short-term to settle inflammation, biologics if DMARDs are not enough, and physiotherapy and occupational therapy. The "treat-to-target" approach — aiming for remission — is the standard of care in the NHS.

Can You Have Both OA and RA?

Yes, it is possible to have both. In fact, this is not uncommon. Someone with long-standing RA may develop secondary OA in the affected joints because of the damage caused by inflammation over time. Diagnosis and treatment of dual conditions require careful management by your rheumatology team.

Getting the Right Diagnosis

If you have joint pain, the most important first step is getting the right diagnosis. Expect a GP assessment (questions about symptoms), a physical examination (feeling joints for swelling, warmth, range of motion), blood tests (inflammatory markers, rheumatoid factor, anti-CCP antibodies), imaging (X-rays showing cartilage loss in OA or joint erosion in RA, ultrasound or MRI for more detail), and referral to a rheumatologist if RA or another inflammatory arthritis is suspected. Early treatment makes a huge difference.

Under the Equality Act 2010, employers in Great Britain should consider reasonable adjustments when arthritis has a substantial long-term effect. title: Arthritis Flare-Ups — How to Recognise, Manage, and Recover
excerpt: Learn how to spot the early signs of an arthritis flare, what to do when one hits, the role of medication, and how to prevent future flare-ups.
content:
Clinically reviewed by Louis Maxwell, First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483. Last updated: June 2026.

Quick answer: An arthritis flare-up is a temporary worsening of arthritis symptoms, which can vary depending on the type of arthritis. It may involve increased pain, stiffness, swelling, and fatigue, lasting from days to several weeks. Early signs include unusual tiredness or increased stiffness. Managing a flare involves resting the affected joint(s), using heat or ice, and taking prescribed medications.

One day you feel steady. The next, your joints are swollen, stiff, and screaming — as if all your progress has been undone overnight. If this sounds familiar, you have experienced an arthritis flare-up. Flare-ups are frightening and frustrating. But they are also part of living with arthritis — and they can be managed. This guide will help you recognise a flare early, take the right steps when it happens, and reduce the chance of future flares.

What Is an Arthritis Flare-Up?

A flare-up (or "flare") is a sudden, temporary worsening of your arthritis symptoms. Instead of your usual background pain, you experience a spike that may last anywhere from a few days to several weeks. Flare-ups happen in all types of arthritis, but they feel different depending on your diagnosis:

  • Osteoarthritis (OA) flares: Often triggered by overuse or injury. Pain increases and the joint may swell. Typically settles within days to a week with rest.
  • Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) flares: Involve increased inflammation — joints become hot, red, swollen, and stiff (especially in the morning). Can last longer and may need medication changes.
  • Gout flares: A specific type of flare caused by urate crystals in the joint. Extremely painful and sudden, often affecting the big toe.

Early Warning Signs of a Flare

Your body often gives you clues before a full flare hits. Learning to spot these warning signs can help you act early:

  • Increased stiffness — especially in the morning, lasting longer than usual
  • Fatigue — unusual tiredness, feeling "drained"
  • Mild swelling or warmth — a joint that feels warmer or puffier than yesterday
  • "Foggy" feeling — trouble concentrating (common in RA flares)
  • Mood changes — feeling low or irritable for no clear reason
  • Reduced range of motion — a joint that does not bend or straighten as far as usual

If you notice these signs, it is time to ease up on activity and focus on self-care — before the flare worsens.

Immediate Steps to Take During a Flare

When a flare hits, the goal shifts from "push through" to "protect and settle." Your action plan:

  1. Pause high-impact activities. Cancel the gym session, the long walk, or heavy housework. Your joints need a break.
  2. But keep moving gently. Complete rest can make joints stiffer. Gentle range-of-motion movements help prevent this.
  3. Use your flare toolkit. Heat packs, ice packs, pain relief, and any flare-management plan you have discussed with your doctor.
  4. Prioritise sleep. Your body heals during rest. Make sleep non-negotiable.
  5. Be kind to yourself. Flares are not a personal failure. They are part of the condition.

Medications That Help During a Flare

What you take depends on your type of arthritis and what your GP or rheumatologist has prescribed. For OA flares: paracetamol or NSAIDs (ibuprofen, naproxen), topical NSAID gel, or a short course of stronger pain relief if prescribed. For RA flares: NSAIDs or COX-2 inhibitors, a temporary increase in corticosteroids as directed, a steroid injection into the affected joint, or a review of your DMARDs if flares become frequent. Do not stop or change your DMARDs or biologics without medical advice.

Rest, Ice, Heat — What Works?

Heat is best for stiff, achy joints (especially OA) — warm bath, heated wheat bag, or heat pad for 15–20 minutes. Ice is best for hot, swollen, inflamed joints (common in RA or gout) — ice pack wrapped in a tea towel for 10–15 minutes, never directly on skin. Rest is appropriate for all types during the acute phase, but avoid total bed rest. Elevate the joint if swollen. Some people find alternating heat and ice helpful — experiment gently.

Preventing Future Flares

You cannot prevent every flare — but you can reduce how often they happen and how severe they become. Pace yourself — break tasks into smaller chunks, alternate activity with rest. Stay active regularly — strong muscles protect joints. Maintain a healthy weight — less load equals less joint stress. Take medication as prescribed — skipping doses invites trouble. Manage stress — stress and inflammation are linked. Eat an anti-inflammatory diet — a Mediterranean-style diet may help reduce background inflammation. Track your flares — keep a simple diary to spot patterns.

When to Contact Your GP or Rheumatologist

Contact your doctor if: the flare lasts more than two weeks without improvement, pain is severe and not responding to usual pain relief, you develop a fever alongside joint pain (could indicate infection), a single joint becomes suddenly very hot, red, and swollen (could be septic arthritis — needs urgent treatment), or you are having flares more than once per month disrupting your life.

Marketing claims for joint supplements often outrun the research. Look for products that state dose clearly, avoid miracle language, and fit alongside — never instead of — prescribed treatment. Stop and seek advice if you notice bruising, stomach pain, yellowing of the skin or new rashes.

title: Knee Joint Supplements UK: Evidence, Limits & Safer Choices
excerpt: Honest UK guide to knee joint supplements: modest evidence for a shortlist of options, quality pitfalls, and why exercise and NHS care still come first.
content:
Quick answer: No supplement rebuilds a worn knee. Evidence is mixed-to-modest for some options people try for knee osteoarthritis — especially pharmaceutical-grade glucosamine sulphate, undenatured type II collagen (UC-II), chondroitin, Boswellia extracts, bioavailable curcumin and higher-dose omega-3 — and weaker or inconsistent for many high-street blends. Treat supplements as optional extras beside exercise, weight advice where relevant, physiotherapy and NHS care. Check interactions with a pharmacist or GP before you start.

Knee pain drives a huge share of arthritis searches in the UK. Marketing often outruns the research. Use this page to prepare questions for your clinician, then confirm any product against your medicines list. For condition basics see the osteoarthritis guide; for movement see the exercise hub and pain-relief guide; for food patterns see the diet hub and our supplements hub.

What supplements can and cannot do

In knee osteoarthritis, cartilage and joint tissues change over years. Supplements do not reverse structural damage the way joint replacement can. At best, some people report modest pain or function changes after weeks to months. Quality varies wildly: dose, chemical form and third-party testing matter more than brand slogans.

Options with more research discussion (still not “cures”)

Glucosamine sulphate

Among joint supplements, glucosamine sulphate (often discussed around 1,500 mg/day of a pharmaceutical-grade sulphate salt) has the longest research trail for knee OA symptoms. Results are mixed; some people notice little change. Hydrochloride forms in cheap blends have often performed less consistently in trials. Shellfish-derived products are unsafe if you have that allergy. See also glucosamine hub.

Undenatured type II collagen (UC-II)

Low-dose undenatured type II collagen (commonly 40 mg/day of a branded UC-II ingredient in trials) is studied for knee symptoms via an immune “oral tolerance” idea. Evidence is growing but not definitive. It is not the same as large doses of hydrolysed collagen peptides.

Chondroitin sulphate

Chondroitin is sometimes combined with glucosamine. European rheumatology discussion has been more favourable than some UK high-street expectations. Source purity and dose (often discussed around 800–1,200 mg/day of sulphate forms) vary; adulteration is a known quality problem.

Boswellia serrata extracts

Standardised Boswellia extracts (look for clear AKBA standardisation on the label) have randomised trial data for knee pain in some studies. “Herbal” does not mean risk-free — tell your clinician, especially if you take other anti-inflammatories or have liver disease.

Bioavailable curcumin

Enhanced-absorption curcumin extracts are not the same as kitchen turmeric. Some knee OA trials suggest modest symptom help over weeks, with fewer stomach issues than NSAIDs for some people — but curcumin can interact with anticoagulants and is unsuitable for everyone. Read turmeric for arthritis and the turmeric supplement page before buying high-dose products.

Omega-3 (EPA + DHA)

Higher intakes of long-chain omega-3s from oily fish or quality fish-oil/algae oils are more about inflammation context than “cartilage rebuild”. Food-first patterns sit in our omega-3 foods guide. High-dose oils can affect bleeding risk — pharmacist check recommended.

Oral hyaluronic acid

Injectable hyaluronic acid is a clinic decision. Oral HA evidence is thinner; treat it as optional and secondary to proven rehab and medical care.

A safer way to experiment

  • Change one product at a time for several weeks so you can judge benefit honestly.
  • Keep a simple pain (0–10), stiffness and walking-distance note.
  • Prefer clear dose labelling and avoid miracle language.
  • Bring the bottle to pharmacy or clinic appointments.
  • Stop and seek advice for bruising, severe stomach pain, yellowing of the skin, breathing problems or new rashes.

What usually matters more than any capsule

NICE-aligned care for osteoarthritis centres on therapeutic exercise and, where appropriate, weight management, plus topical or oral medicines discussed with your team. Supplements sit beside — never instead of — that plan. If daily living or mobility costs are a concern, use the Benefits & PIP hub. Newly diagnosed? Start at newly diagnosed.

Quick questions

Is there a single “best” knee supplement? No honest ranking fits every person. Evidence is strongest as a conversation about a shortlist, not a league table.

Can I combine several? Combining raises cost and interaction risk. Discuss stacks with a pharmacist first.

How long before I judge? Many trials look at weeks to months. Worsening pain, swelling with fever, or sudden locking needs clinical review sooner.

Educational information for people in the United Kingdom — not personal medical advice or a product endorsement.

title: Gout Medication UK: A Complete Guide to Drugs for Gout
excerpt: From managing a gout attack to long-term uric acid control — everything you need to know about gout treatment in the UK.
content:
Quick answer: For acute gout attacks, common treatments include NSAIDs like naproxen (500mg twice daily) or indomethacin, which reduce inflammation and pain. Colchicine, taken as 1mg initially then 500 micrograms one hour later, is an alternative, especially if NSAIDs are unsuitable. If these are ineffective, corticosteroids such as prednisolone (30-35mg daily for 3-5 days) can be used.

Gout is the most common form of inflammatory arthritis in the UK, affecting an estimated 2.5 million people — and rates have been rising for decades. A gout attack is one of the most painful medical events a person can experience: the intense burning, swelling, and redness, typically in the big toe but potentially in any joint, can be completely debilitating.

The good news is that gout is one of the most treatable forms of arthritis. With the right gout medication in the UK, attacks can be stopped quickly, and with consistent long-term treatment, many people become entirely gout-free. This guide covers everything from how gout develops, to the drugs used to treat acute attacks, to the urate-lowering therapies available to UK patients.

Understanding Gout: Why Medication Is Needed

Gout is caused by hyperuricaemia — elevated levels of uric acid in the blood. When uric acid exceeds its solubility threshold (approximately 360 micromol/L), it crystallises as monosodium urate (MSU) crystals in joint spaces and surrounding tissue. These sharp, needle-like crystals trigger an intense immune response, producing the extreme pain and inflammation of a gout attack.

Without treatment, gout attacks become more frequent and eventually chronic. Crystals can also accumulate in soft tissue (tophi), damage kidneys, and cause cardiovascular complications. This is why long-term medication to control uric acid levels — not just treating individual attacks — is essential for most people with recurrent gout.

Medications for Acute Gout Attacks

The priority during an acute gout attack is to reduce pain and inflammation as quickly as possible. Three types of medication are used.

NSAIDs (Non-Steroidal Anti-Inflammatory Drugs)

NSAIDs are usually the first-line treatment for acute gout in the UK. Naproxen (500 mg twice daily) and indomethacin are the most commonly prescribed. They work by inhibiting COX enzymes and reducing prostaglandin production, thereby rapidly reducing inflammation and pain. Most people notice significant improvement within 24 hours.

NSAIDs must be used with caution or avoided in people with kidney disease, stomach ulcers, heart failure, or who are taking anticoagulants. Always take NSAIDs with food. Naproxen is available over the counter in the UK at lower doses; higher prescription doses provide greater anti-inflammatory effect.

Colchicine

Colchicine is a plant-derived drug — originally extracted from the autumn crocus — that has been used for gout for over a century. It works by disrupting microtubule function in neutrophils, preventing them from migrating to the inflamed joint and releasing inflammatory mediators.

Modern UK guidelines (BSR and EULAR) recommend low-dose colchicine: 1 mg initially, followed by 500 micrograms one hour later. This low-dose regimen is as effective as the older high-dose approach but with significantly fewer gastrointestinal side effects (nausea, diarrhoea, abdominal cramping). Colchicine is particularly useful for people who cannot tolerate NSAIDs.

Important drug interactions for colchicine

  • Statins (increased risk of muscle damage — myopathy).
  • Ciclosporin (significantly increased colchicine levels — avoid combination).
  • Clarithromycin and other macrolide antibiotics.
  • Always inform your GP and pharmacist of all medications you take.

Corticosteroids

When NSAIDs and colchicine are contraindicated or ineffective, oral corticosteroids (typically prednisolone 30–35 mg daily for 3–5 days) are highly effective for acute gout. Intra-articular steroid injections directly into the affected joint provide rapid, targeted relief and are particularly useful for large joints such as the knee or ankle.

Corticosteroids should not be used long-term for gout due to well-known side effects including blood sugar elevation, bone thinning, weight gain, and adrenal suppression.

Long-Term Urate-Lowering Therapy (ULT)

After a confirmed gout diagnosis — particularly with two or more attacks per year, tophi, kidney stones, or chronic kidney disease — UK guidelines recommend starting urate-lowering therapy to permanently reduce uric acid levels. The target is to keep serum urate below 360 micromol/L (and below 300 micromol/L in those with tophi).

Allopurinol — The Gold Standard

Allopurinol is the first-line ULT in the UK and worldwide. It is a xanthine oxidase inhibitor, meaning it blocks the enzyme responsible for the final step in uric acid production. Starting at 100 mg daily and gradually titrating upward (typically to 300 mg, sometimes higher), allopurinol effectively reduces uric acid in the majority of patients.

A key principle: allopurinol must always be started after an acute attack has fully resolved (usually two to four weeks after), never during one, as starting it during an attack can paradoxically prolong or worsen the flare. A prophylactic dose of colchicine (500 mcg once or twice daily) is typically prescribed for the first six months of allopurinol therapy to prevent this.

Allopurinol is generally well tolerated. Rare but serious reactions include allopurinol hypersensitivity syndrome (AHS) — a potentially life-threatening skin reaction. Risk is higher in people of Han Chinese, Thai, and Korean descent, who should be tested for the HLA-B*5801 allele before starting treatment.

Febuxostat — An Alternative for Allopurinol Intolerance

Febuxostat (brand name Adenuric in the UK) is a non-purine xanthine oxidase inhibitor, available in the UK for people who cannot tolerate or do not respond adequately to allopurinol. It is often more potent than standard allopurinol doses and does not require dose adjustment for mild-to-moderate kidney impairment.

A 2019 clinical trial (CARES trial) raised concerns about cardiovascular mortality with febuxostat versus allopurinol, though subsequent European analyses have not replicated this finding. In the UK, febuxostat should be used with caution in people with established cardiovascular disease.

Benzbromarone and Other Uricosurics

Uricosuric drugs work differently — instead of reducing uric acid production, they increase its excretion via the kidneys. Benzbromarone is available on a named-patient basis in the UK for patients who overproduce uric acid or have failed other treatments. Probenecid is another option. These drugs are contraindicated in kidney stone formers as they increase urinary urate and the risk of stone formation.

Quick Answer

For acute gout attacks, UK doctors prescribe NSAIDs (naproxen, indomethacin), low-dose colchicine, or corticosteroids. For long-term prevention, urate-lowering therapy with allopurinol (first-line) or febuxostat is recommended. The target is to keep serum urate below 360 micromol/L. Medication should always be managed by a GP or rheumatologist.

Lifestyle Measures Alongside Medication

Medication is most effective when supported by lifestyle changes: staying well hydrated (aim for 2–3 litres of fluid daily), reducing beer and spirits, limiting red meat and seafood high in purines, avoiding fructose-rich drinks, achieving a healthy weight, and taking any prescribed diuretics (water tablets) only as directed by your doctor, as these can raise uric acid levels.

Conclusion

Gout is eminently treatable and, with the right medication and lifestyle management, entirely preventable. If you are experiencing recurrent attacks, speak to your GP about starting urate-lowering therapy. Do not wait — untreated gout causes cumulative joint damage that can be difficult to reverse.

title: Joint Replacement Surgery for Arthritis — A Complete UK Guide
excerpt: Everything you need to know about knee and hip replacement surgery on the NHS: when it's right, what to expect, and how to prepare and recover.
content:
Clinically reviewed by Louis Maxwell, First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483. Last updated: June 2026.

Quick answer: Joint replacement surgery is considered when severe, persistent pain affects daily activities and sleep, other treatments have failed, X-rays show significant joint damage, and quality of life is impacted. In the UK, over 200,000 hip and knee replacements occur annually, and more than 90% of people report significant improvement in pain and mobility.

Joint replacement surgery sounds daunting. It is natural to feel anxious — but it is also one of the most successful operations in modern medicine. In the UK, more than 200,000 hip and knee replacements are performed each year, and over 90% of people report significant improvement in pain and mobility.

This guide explains everything in plain English, from deciding if surgery is right for you to what recovery actually feels like.

When Is Joint Replacement the Right Choice?

Joint replacement is not the first option. You and your doctor will usually consider it when you have severe persistent pain affecting your sleep and daily activities, other treatments have not provided enough relief, X-rays show significant joint damage, and your quality of life is being seriously affected. It is a decision you make with your orthopaedic surgeon, not one they make for you.

Knee Replacement Surgery — What to Expect

A total knee replacement (knee arthroplasty) involves removing the damaged surfaces of the knee joint and replacing them with metal and plastic implants. The operation takes about 1–2 hours, usually under spinal anaesthetic or general anaesthetic. You will typically stay in hospital for 1–3 days. You will be encouraged to stand and take a few steps with a walking frame within 24 hours, and a physiotherapist will guide you through the first exercises. Most people notice improved mobility within 6–12 weeks, with continued gains for up to a year.

Hip Replacement Surgery — Recovery and Results

Hip replacements follow a similar pattern to knee replacements. The damaged ball-and-socket joint is replaced with artificial components. Hip replacement generally has a slightly quicker early recovery than knee replacement. Many people go home within 1–2 days. Use crutches or a walking frame for 2–6 weeks, follow hip precautions if advised, and most people can drive after about 6 weeks (check with your insurance provider). You may return to work within 6–12 weeks depending on your job.

Getting on the NHS Waiting List

The pathway typically involves GP referral to an orthopaedic consultant, specialist assessment with X-ray review, decision to proceed, pre-operative assessment (blood tests, heart tracing, health checks), and finally a surgery date. The NHS Constitution target is a maximum of 18 weeks from referral to treatment, but waits may be longer in some areas.

Preparing for Surgery (Pre-habilitation)

What you do before surgery significantly affects how well you recover after. Strengthen your muscles around the joint — stronger muscles mean faster recovery. Maintain a healthy weight — excess weight puts extra stress on your new joint and increases surgical risks. Stop smoking — it slows healing and raises complication risks. Eat well, and plan your home: arrange help with shopping, cooking, and transport for the first few weeks, and clear trip hazards.

Recovery Timeline and Rehabilitation

Everyone recovers at their own pace. Week 1–2: walking with a frame or crutches inside the house, daily physio exercises, swelling and discomfort peak then improve. Weeks 2–6: gradually reduce walking aids, start walking outside, continue exercises. Weeks 6–12: walking freely, return to driving, may return to office-based work. 3–6 months: significant improvement in pain and function. 6–12 months: continued gains, resume low-impact sports. Knee replacements tend to have a slightly slower recovery than hips.

Life After Joint Replacement

The goal is a life with less pain and more movement. Most people can walk without pain, sleep through the night, return to hobbies like gardening and swimming, and travel comfortably. You should avoid high-impact activities like running or jumping. Modern implants often last 15–25 years or more.

Alternatives to Surgery

Surgery is not the only way forward. Some people manage well with weight loss (even 5–10% of body weight can significantly reduce knee pain), a tailored physiotherapy exercise programme, a pain management programme combining physical and psychological strategies, walking aids and supports, or steroid injections for temporary relief. Always explore these with your GP or physiotherapist first.

Food-first is usually safer than stacking capsules. If you do try a supplement, choose a reputable UK brand, check for interactions with your medicines (especially blood thinners), and give any trial a clear stop date so you can judge whether symptoms truly changed.

title: The Best Foods to Eat for Arthritis: Your Anti-Inflammatory Diet
excerpt: For arthritis management, aim for an anti-inflammatory diet rich in oily fish, extra-virgin olive oil, leafy green vegetables, berries, walnuts, and alliums…
content:
Quick answer: For arthritis management, aim for an anti-inflammatory diet rich in oily fish, extra-virgin olive oil, leafy green vegetables, berries, walnuts, and alliums like garlic. Oily fish like salmon and mackerel provide omega-3s, while EVOO contains anti-inflammatory oleocanthal. These foods can help reduce inflammation and improve joint health.

There is no magic food that cures arthritis. But there is robust and growing evidence that what you put on your plate has a direct effect on systemic inflammation — the underlying mechanism behind most forms of joint disease. Adding the right foods to your diet is just as important as removing the wrong ones.

This article brings together the best-evidenced anti-inflammatory foods for people living with arthritis in the UK. It covers practical ways to incorporate them into a British diet without expensive ingredients or complicated recipes. Whether you have osteoarthritis, rheumatoid arthritis, psoriatic arthritis, or ankylosing spondylitis, an anti-inflammatory eating pattern can make a real difference.

The Anti-Inflammatory Diet Principle

The Mediterranean diet is the most studied dietary pattern for arthritis and inflammation. Rich in plant foods, oily fish, olive oil, and whole grains, it has been shown in multiple clinical trials to reduce CRP (C-reactive protein, a key inflammation marker), lower TNF-alpha levels, and improve pain and function scores in people with RA and OA.

You do not need to move to Greece to benefit. The principles — more vegetables, more fish, more olive oil, less processed food — translate perfectly to a UK shopping basket.

1. Oily Fish

Oily fish — salmon, mackerel, sardines, herring, trout, and anchovies — are the single most powerful anti-inflammatory food you can add to your arthritis diet. They are the richest natural sources of long-chain omega-3 fatty acids EPA and DHA, which suppress inflammatory cytokines and reduce joint tenderness and morning stiffness.

UK guidance recommends eating at least two portions of fish per week, one of which should be oily. For arthritis management, aiming for three to four portions weekly is reasonable. Tinned sardines, mackerel, and salmon are budget-friendly options widely available in UK supermarkets and just as nutritious as fresh fish.

Easy UK meal ideas

  • Tinned sardines on wholegrain toast — quick, cheap, and rich in omega-3.
  • Grilled salmon fillet with sweet potato and steamed broccoli.
  • Smoked mackerel pâté with oatcakes and cucumber.

2. Extra-Virgin Olive Oil

Extra-virgin olive oil (EVOO) is a cornerstone of the Mediterranean diet and arguably the most important fat for people with arthritis. It contains oleocanthal, a polyphenol that inhibits COX-1 and COX-2 enzymes — the same enzymes blocked by ibuprofen. Research from the University of Pennsylvania calculated that 3.4 tablespoons of EVOO provides anti-inflammatory activity equivalent to approximately 10% of a standard ibuprofen dose.

EVOO also contains hydroxytyrosol and oleuropein, potent antioxidants that protect joint tissue from oxidative stress. Use EVOO as your primary cooking fat, in salad dressings, and drizzled over cooked vegetables. Choose bottles labelled 'cold-pressed' and 'first cold extraction' for maximum polyphenol content.

3. Leafy Green Vegetables

Spinach, kale, Swiss chard, rocket, and spring greens are nutritional powerhouses for arthritis. They are rich in antioxidants — including vitamins C and E, and the carotenoids lutein and zeaxanthin — that neutralise the free radicals produced during inflammation, protecting cartilage and synovial tissue from further damage.

Kale and spinach are also excellent sources of vitamin K, which plays a role in bone metabolism and may slow OA progression. A Harvard study found that people with the highest vitamin K intakes had significantly lower rates of knee and hip OA. Aim for two to three portions of leafy greens per day, either raw in salads or lightly steamed.

4. Berries and Cherries

Berries are among the richest dietary sources of anthocyanins — the dark red and blue pigments that give blueberries, blackberries, and cherries their colour. Anthocyanins are potent antioxidants that have been shown to inhibit inflammatory enzymes and reduce CRP levels.

Tart cherry, in particular, has remarkable evidence for gout. Multiple randomised controlled trials have shown that tart cherry juice or concentrate significantly reduces gout flare frequency and lowers serum uric acid levels. A study published in Arthritis and Rheumatism found that two servings of cherries per day were associated with a 35% lower risk of gout attacks. Fresh or frozen blueberries, strawberries, and blackcurrants provide similar anthocyanin benefits for other arthritis types.

5. Walnuts and Other Nuts

Walnuts are unique among nuts in that they are an excellent plant-based source of ALA (alpha-linolenic acid), the precursor to omega-3 fatty acids. They also contain ellagic acid, an anti-inflammatory polyphenol. A study in the Journal of the American College of Nutrition found that people with RA who consumed walnuts regularly reported lower disease activity scores.

Other beneficial nuts include almonds (rich in vitamin E, which protects joint membranes from oxidative damage), Brazil nuts (rich in selenium, a deficiency of which is associated with increased RA activity), and pistachios. A small handful — about 30g — five times per week is a practical and cost-effective target.

6. Garlic, Onions, and the Allium Family

Garlic, onions, leeks, and spring onions belong to the allium family and contain diallyl disulfide, a compound that inhibits the activity of pro-inflammatory cytokines including IL-17. Research from King's College London found that women who regularly ate a diet rich in alliums had significantly less hip OA than those who did not.

Garlic is also a powerful antimicrobial and prebiotic, supporting the gut microbiome — increasingly recognised as a key modulator of systemic inflammation. Use fresh garlic liberally in cooking, and do not overlook leeks and onions as anti-inflammatory staples.

7. Pulses and Legumes

Lentils, chickpeas, black beans, kidney beans, and peas are fibre-rich, plant-based proteins that support a healthy gut microbiome and provide a slow, sustained energy release that avoids the blood sugar spikes associated with inflammation. They are also rich in folate, magnesium, and iron — nutrients important for joint and bone health.

UK arthritis charities recommend two to three portions of pulses per week. Tinned chickpeas and lentils are convenient, affordable, and nutritionally equivalent to dried versions. Add them to curries, soups, stews, and salads for a practical, anti-inflammatory protein boost.

8. Green Tea

Green tea contains epigallocatechin-3-gallate (EGCG), one of the most potent polyphenols studied for arthritis. Laboratory studies show EGCG inhibits the production of inflammatory cytokines and matrix metalloproteinases — enzymes that break down cartilage. Human studies have found associations between habitual green tea consumption and lower rates of RA and OA in Asian populations.

Three to four cups of green tea per day provides a meaningful dose of EGCG. Matcha powder, which contains the whole ground tea leaf, delivers roughly ten times the EGCG of a regular green tea bag. Avoid adding milk, which may bind the polyphenols and reduce absorption.

Quick Answer

The best foods for arthritis are oily fish (salmon, mackerel, sardines), extra-virgin olive oil, leafy green vegetables (spinach, kale), berries and tart cherries, walnuts, garlic and onions, pulses and legumes, and green tea. These foods reduce inflammation, protect joint tissue, and are backed by clinical research.

Building Your Anti-Arthritis Plate

A practical target: fill half your plate with colourful vegetables at every meal, include oily fish three times per week, use olive oil instead of butter or vegetable oil, snack on a small handful of walnuts or berries, and drink green tea in place of one or two daily coffees. Small, consistent changes compounded over weeks and months produce lasting results.

Conclusion

The best foods to eat for arthritis share a common theme: they are whole, minimally processed, and rich in anti-inflammatory compounds. An evidence-based eating pattern centred on oily fish, olive oil, colourful vegetables, berries, nuts, and pulses can meaningfully reduce pain, lower inflammation markers, and protect joint tissue over time. Pair these dietary changes with your prescribed treatment, regular appropriate exercise, and regular GP reviews for the best possible outcome.

title: Arthritis Medication — What Works, What to Expect
excerpt: A clear, plain-English guide to arthritis medications: painkillers, NSAIDs, DMARDs, biologics, corticosteroids, and how to get them on the NHS.
content:
Clinically reviewed by Louis Maxwell, First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483. Last updated: June 2026.

Quick answer: Arthritis medications include painkillers like paracetamol and stronger opioids for severe pain. NSAIDs such as ibuprofen reduce both pain and inflammation. DMARDs and biologics treat underlying disease processes in inflammatory arthritis. Corticosteroids offer potent anti-inflammatory effects. Topical gels and creams can provide localised relief. Most are available on NHS prescription.

Taking medication for arthritis can feel like navigating a maze. There are so many names, so many warnings — and you just want something that helps.

This guide explains every major type of arthritis medication in plain English. We cover what each one does, how it works, potential side effects, and how to get it on the NHS. Always speak to your GP or rheumatologist before starting or stopping any medication.

Painkillers (Paracetamol, Codeine) for Arthritis

Paracetamol

Paracetamol is often the first painkiller your GP will suggest. It helps with mild-to-moderate pain and is generally safe when taken at the recommended dose (no more than 4g, or eight 500mg tablets, in 24 hours). Widely available, few side effects, inexpensive — but it does not reduce inflammation and may not be strong enough for severe pain.

Codeine and Other Opioids

Codeine, tramadol, and morphine-based drugs are stronger painkillers sometimes prescribed for short periods when pain is severe. Important warning: These medicines can cause dependence. The NHS recommends using the lowest effective dose for the shortest possible time. Common side effects include constipation, drowsiness, and nausea.

NSAIDs — Ibuprofen, Naproxen, and Cox-2 Inhibitors

NSAIDs (non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs) relieve both pain and inflammation. They are widely used for osteoarthritis, rheumatoid arthritis, and other types.

  • Traditional NSAIDs: Ibuprofen, Naproxen, Diclofenac — available over the counter or on prescription.
  • Cox-2 inhibitors: Celecoxib, Etoricoxib — prescription-only; may be gentler on the stomach.

Potential side effects: NSAIDs can irritate the stomach lining. Your GP may prescribe a stomach-protecting drug (proton pump inhibitor, or PPI) alongside them. Long-term use at high doses may affect kidney function or blood pressure. People with asthma, stomach ulcers, kidney problems, or heart conditions should speak to their GP before taking NSAIDs.

DMARDs for Inflammatory Arthritis

DMARDs (disease-modifying anti-rheumatic drugs) treat the underlying disease process in rheumatoid arthritis — they aim to slow or stop the immune system from attacking the joints. Common DMARDs include:

  • Methotrexate — Usually the first DMARD prescribed for RA. Taken once a week (not daily). Regular blood tests needed.
  • Sulfasalazine — Often used when methotrexate is not suitable or in combination with it.
  • Leflunomide — Another alternative or add-on DMARD.
  • Hydroxychloroquine — Milder DMARD, sometimes used for milder RA or lupus.

Key facts: They take 6–12 weeks to work. Regular blood monitoring is essential. They can affect the immune system, increasing infection risk. Stopping suddenly can cause a flare-up.

Biologics — Newer Treatments for RA

Biologics are a newer class of DMARD, made from living cells. They target very specific parts of the immune system involved in inflammation. Examples include Adalimumab (Humira), Etanercept (Enbrel), Infliximab (Remicade), and Tocilizumab (RoActemra). On the NHS, they are usually offered to people whose RA has not responded well to at least two standard DMARDs and whose disease activity remains high. They are given by injection or infusion and require careful monitoring.

Corticosteroid Injections and Tablets

Corticosteroids (often simply called "steroids") are powerful anti-inflammatories — not the same as anabolic steroids misused in sport. Steroid injections delivered directly into a painful joint can provide rapid relief lasting weeks to months (limit of 3–4 per year in the same joint). Steroid tablets (prednisolone) are used for short courses during severe flares or low-dose long-term control, though long-term use carries risks including weight gain, osteoporosis, and high blood pressure.

Topical Treatments (Gels and Creams)

Topical NSAIDs — ibuprofen gel or diclofenac gel — are applied directly to the skin over a painful joint. They cause fewer stomach side effects than tablets, deliver medication exactly where needed, and are available over the counter. Topical capsaicin cream (from chilli peppers) works by reducing substance P, a chemical that sends pain signals — it can take a few weeks of regular use to show benefit.

Getting Arthritis Medication on the NHS

Most arthritis medications are available on NHS prescription. Over-the-counter drugs (paracetamol, ibuprofen gel, low-dose ibuprofen tablets) can be bought yourself — buying paracetamol in bulk is often cheaper than a prescription. Prescription NSAIDs, DMARDs, biologics, and steroids are prescribed by your GP or rheumatologist at the standard NHS prescription charge (£9.90 per item as of 2024/25), unless you qualify for free prescriptions. If you need regular medication, a Prescription Prepayment Certificate (PPC) costs around £32 for three months of unlimited prescriptions.

Talking to Your GP About Medication

  1. Be specific about your pain. "I struggle to open jars and my hands hurt every morning for an hour" is more helpful than "I'm in pain."
  2. Mention what you have already tried. Include exercise, over-the-counter medication, and lifestyle changes.
  3. Ask questions. Write them down beforehand.
  4. Discuss side effects openly. If a medicine makes you feel unwell, say so. There are usually alternatives.
  5. Do not stop medication suddenly. Some drugs (especially steroids) need to be reduced gradually under medical supervision.

In many areas you can ask your NHS trust about self-referral to physiotherapy or lifestyle support without waiting for a hospital letter. Check your GP surgery website or the NHS App for the route that applies where you live.

Benefits conversations

Personal Independence Payment (PIP) looks at how your condition affects daily living and mobility, not the diagnosis name alone. Keep a short diary of bad days, help you need with dressing or cooking, and walking limits. Welfare rights advisers at local councils or charities can check forms before you submit them.

Work, rights and practical adjustments

Under the Equality Act 2010, employers in Great Britain should consider reasonable adjustments when arthritis has a substantial long-term effect. That can mean flexible hours, more breaks, seating, parking closer to the entrance, or software that reduces typing strain. Acas and Citizens Advice both publish plain-English guides you can take into a meeting.

Preparing for appointments

Write three priorities before you go: main symptom, functional limit (stairs, sleep, work), and the question you most need answered. Bring a current medicine list including over-the-counter products. If English is not your first language, request an interpreter when you book.

Working with NHS pathways

Most people start with GP care, community physiotherapy and self-management, with rheumatology involved when inflammatory disease is suspected or treatment needs escalate. Ask what monitoring blood tests or reviews you should expect, and who to contact between appointments if a flare escalates.

Pacing on good and bad days

On better days it is tempting to catch up on everything at once. Spread chores and exercise across the week instead. Use the two-hour rule many physiotherapists suggest: if pain or fatigue is clearly worse two hours after activity, the dose was too high — trim the next session rather than stopping altogether.

Quick questions about Arthritis Medication What Works

Is this a substitute for seeing a clinician? No. Use it to prepare questions and understand options, then confirm decisions with your NHS team.

How long before I judge whether a change helped? Give most habit or exercise changes at least two to four weeks, unless pain or swelling clearly worsens — in that case scale back sooner.

What should I track? Joint pain (0–10), morning stiffness time, sleep quality, and how far you can walk or how long you can type or stand. Patterns beat one-off ratings.

Safety and when to get urgent help

This page is general information for people in the United Kingdom, not personal medical advice. Seek urgent help via NHS 111 or A&E if you have sudden inability to move a joint, hot swollen joint with fever, chest pain, severe shortness of breath, or symptoms that feel immediately dangerous.

title: Arthritis Treatment — Your Complete Guide to Managing Joint Pain
excerpt: Explore every treatment option for arthritis, from NHS pathways and exercise to medication, physiotherapy, surgery, and complementary therapies.
content:
Clinically reviewed by Louis Maxwell, First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483. Last updated: June 2026.

Quick answer: Arthritis treatment involves a combination of approaches to manage symptoms. Key options include exercise and movement (recommended as a first-line treatment), weight management, physiotherapy, occupational therapy, and various medications for pain and inflammation. Surgery may be considered for severe cases when other treatments are insufficient. Complementary therapies can also provide additional relief. Always discuss treatment choices with your GP.

Living with arthritis means living with questions. What will help? Where do I start? Am I doing enough?

We understand. More than 10 million people in the UK live with arthritis — you are not alone. And while there is currently no cure, there is a great deal you can do to manage your symptoms and live well.

This guide walks you through every treatment option available on the NHS and beyond. Think of it as your map. You don't need to take every path; just the ones that are right for you.

What Treatment Options Are Available for Arthritis?

Arthritis treatment is not a single thing. It is a combination of approaches that work together. The National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) — the body that advises the NHS on best practice — recommends a stepped approach, starting with the safest, most proven options first.

The main categories are:

  • Exercise and movement (NICE's first-line treatment)
  • Weight management (if needed)
  • Physiotherapy and occupational therapy
  • Pain-relieving medications
  • Disease-modifying drugs (for inflammatory types like rheumatoid arthritis)
  • Surgery (when other options are no longer enough)
  • Complementary and lifestyle approaches

Most people benefit from a mix of several of these.

NHS Treatment Pathway for Arthritis

When you first visit your GP with joint pain, here is what the typical NHS pathway looks like:

  1. GP assessment — Your doctor will ask about your symptoms, examine your joints, and may arrange blood tests or X-rays.
  2. Diagnosis — You may be diagnosed with osteoarthritis (OA), rheumatoid arthritis (RA), or another form.
  3. First-line treatment — You will be offered advice on exercise, weight management, and pain relief. You may be referred to a physiotherapist.
  4. Ongoing management — If symptoms continue, your GP may prescribe stronger medication or refer you to a specialist (rheumatologist or orthopaedic surgeon).
  5. Surgery — In some cases, joint replacement surgery is considered when other treatments have not provided enough relief.

You have the right to be involved in every decision. The NHS calls this "shared decision-making."

Exercise and Movement as Treatment (NICE First-Line)

It may feel counter-intuitive to move a painful joint, but exercise is the single most effective treatment for arthritis. NICE guidelines are clear: exercise should be the first thing offered to everyone with osteoarthritis — before medication.

Here is why:

  • It strengthens the muscles that support your joints
  • It reduces stiffness and improves range of motion
  • It helps maintain a healthy weight, reducing load on weight-bearing joints
  • It releases natural pain-relieving chemicals called endorphins

What kind of exercise? Anything that gets you moving gently — walking, swimming, cycling, yoga, tai chi, or specific physio exercises. The key is to start small and build slowly. Even five minutes a day is a win.

Medications for Arthritis Pain and Inflammation

Medication can help you stay active and comfortable. What you need depends on your diagnosis and the severity of your symptoms.

For Pain Relief

  • Paracetamol — Often tried first. Helps with mild-to-moderate pain, though it does not reduce inflammation.
  • NSAIDs (ibuprofen or naproxen) — Reduce both pain and inflammation. Available as tablets or gels.
  • Opioids (codeine-based) — Sometimes used for short periods of severe pain. Carry a risk of dependence and are used cautiously.

For Inflammatory Arthritis

  • DMARDs (methotrexate, sulfasalazine) — Treat the underlying disease process in RA, not just symptoms.
  • Biologics — Newer targeted treatments for RA that has not responded to standard DMARDs.
  • Corticosteroids — Powerful anti-inflammatories taken as tablets or injected directly into a joint.

Physiotherapy and Occupational Therapy

A physiotherapist is a movement expert. They can assess your movement and strength, design a personalised exercise programme, teach you how to protect your joints, and offer hands-on treatment and pain relief advice. You can access NHS physiotherapy through your GP or by self-referring directly in many areas.

An occupational therapist (OT) helps you do the things that matter to you — work, hobbies, daily tasks. They might suggest joint protection techniques, gadgets and tools to make life easier, or changes to your home or workplace.

Surgery for Arthritis — When Is It Needed?

Surgery is not a first choice. It is considered when you have severe persistent pain that limits your daily life, other treatments have not helped enough, and your joint is significantly damaged. The most common operations are total hip replacement, total knee replacement, and less commonly shoulder or ankle replacement. Joint replacement surgery has excellent outcomes — the vast majority experience significant pain relief and better mobility.

Complementary and Lifestyle Treatments

Many people find additional relief from acupuncture (some evidence for short-term pain relief), massage therapy, heat and cold therapy, mindfulness and relaxation, and dietary changes like a Mediterranean-style diet. Always speak to your GP before starting any complementary therapy.

Creating Your Personal Treatment Plan

  1. Start with movement — What gentle activity can you do today?
  2. Talk to your GP — Be honest about your pain. Bring a list of questions.
  3. Explore physiotherapy — Ask for a referral or self-refer.
  4. Review your diet and weight — Small changes add up.
  5. Build your toolkit — Heat packs, supportive shoes, a TENS machine? Find what works.
  6. Stay informed — Read the other guides on this site. Knowledge is power.

Using evidence carefully

Marketing claims for joint supplements often outrun the research. Look for products that state dose clearly, avoid miracle language, and fit alongside — never instead of — prescribed treatment. Stop and seek advice if you notice bruising, stomach pain, yellowing of the skin or new rashes.
