title: Shoulder Arthritis Exercises: A Complete UK Physiotherapy Guide
excerpt: UK physiotherapist-approved exercises for shoulder arthritis. Step-by-step strengthening, range-of-motion and stretching exercises to reduce pain and improve mobility.
content:
Shoulder arthritis affects approximately one in three people over 60 in the UK to some degree, making it one of the most common causes of shoulder pain and restricted movement. Whether you have osteoarthritis, rheumatoid arthritis or post-traumatic arthritis of the shoulder, targeted exercises can significantly reduce pain, improve range of motion and help you maintain independence for daily tasks like dressing, reaching and driving. This guide provides UK physiotherapist-approved exercises specifically designed for shoulder arthritis.

Quick answer: Shoulder arthritis exercises can significantly reduce pain and improve movement, benefiting conditions like osteoarthritis, rheumatoid arthritis, or post-traumatic arthritis. Key exercises include pendulum swings, wall crawls, and behind-the-back reaches to improve range of motion. Gentle strengthening can be achieved with resistance band external rotations, shoulder blade squeezes, and wall press-ups. Always warm up, move gently, and stop if you experience sharp or worsening pain.

Understanding Shoulder Arthritis

The shoulder is the most mobile joint in the body, with an extraordinary range of motion that allows you to reach, lift, throw and rotate your arm in almost any direction. This mobility comes at a cost — the shoulder relies heavily on muscles, tendons and ligaments for stability rather than bony architecture, making it vulnerable to wear, injury and arthritis.

There are two joints in the shoulder complex that can be affected by arthritis: the glenohumeral joint (the main ball-and-socket joint where the upper arm meets the shoulder blade) and the acromioclavicular (AC) joint (where the collarbone meets the top of the shoulder blade). AC joint arthritis is particularly common and often causes pain when reaching across the body or overhead.

Symptoms of Shoulder Arthritis

  • Deep, aching pain in the shoulder joint, often worse at night
  • Stiffness, particularly in the morning or after periods of inactivity
  • Reduced range of motion — difficulty reaching behind your back, overhead or across your body
  • Grinding, clicking or crepitus during movement
  • Pain with activities like dressing, washing hair, reaching shelves or driving
  • Weakness in the affected arm

Before You Start: Important Guidelines

  • Warm up first — apply a warm flannel or heat pack to the shoulder for 10 minutes before exercising
  • Move gently — never force a painful movement. Work within your comfortable range
  • Consistency beats intensity — daily gentle exercise is better than occasional vigorous sessions
  • Pain monitoring — mild discomfort during exercise is acceptable, but sharp or worsening pain means stop
  • If pain persists more than 2 hours after exercising, you've done too much — reduce intensity next time
  • Consult your GP or physiotherapist before starting if you've had recent shoulder surgery or injection

Range-of-Motion Exercises

These exercises aim to maintain or improve the movement available in your shoulder joint. Perform each exercise 5–10 times, twice daily.

1. Pendulum Swings

Lean forward with your good hand on a table for support. Let the affected arm hang freely. Gently swing the arm in small circles — clockwise for 30 seconds, then anticlockwise for 30 seconds. Gradually increase the circle size as comfort allows. You can hold a small tin of beans (400g) to add gentle traction. This exercise uses gravity to decompress the joint and is excellent for warming up.

2. Wall Crawl (Forward)

Stand facing a wall at arm's length. Place the fingertips of your affected hand on the wall at waist height. Slowly "crawl" your fingers up the wall as high as comfortable. Hold at the top for 5 seconds, then crawl back down. Mark your progress with a small piece of tape — this gives you a visual target to work towards over weeks.

3. Wall Crawl (Side)

Stand sideways to the wall with your affected shoulder closest. Repeat the crawling motion out to the side. This targets a different plane of movement (abduction) that is often restricted in shoulder arthritis.

4. Behind-the-Back Reach

Hold a towel behind your back with both hands — the good arm reaches over the shoulder, the affected arm reaches up from below. Gently pull upward with the good arm to guide the affected arm into a stretch. Hold for 10–15 seconds. This mimics the movement needed for fastening a bra, tucking in a shirt or reaching a back pocket.

5. Cross-Body Stretch

Use your good arm to gently pull the affected arm across your body at chest height. You should feel a stretch at the back and side of the shoulder. Hold for 15–20 seconds. This targets the posterior capsule, which often tightens in shoulder arthritis.

Strengthening Exercises

Once range of motion improves, gentle strengthening helps support and protect the joint. Use light resistance bands (available from pharmacies and online, £5–£15) or small weights (0.5–1 kg to start).

1. Isometric External Rotation

Stand sideways to a wall with the affected arm closest. Bend your elbow to 90 degrees and place the back of your hand against the wall. Push gently into the wall (as if trying to rotate your arm outward) and hold for 10 seconds. This strengthens the rotator cuff without moving the painful joint. Repeat 10 times.

2. Resistance Band External Rotation

Anchor a resistance band at elbow height (a door handle works well). Hold the band with the affected arm, elbow bent to 90 degrees and tucked into your side. Rotate your forearm outward against the band's resistance, then slowly return. Keep the elbow glued to your side throughout. Perform 2 sets of 10 repetitions.

3. Shoulder Blade Squeezes

Sit or stand with good posture. Squeeze your shoulder blades together as if trying to hold a pencil between them. Hold for 5 seconds, then relax. This strengthens the muscles that stabilise the shoulder blade, providing a better foundation for shoulder movement. Repeat 15 times.

4. Wall Press-Up

Stand an arm's length from a wall, hands at shoulder height. Slowly bend your elbows to lean towards the wall, then push back. This gently strengthens the chest and front shoulder muscles. Perform 2 sets of 10 repetitions. Progress by standing further from the wall.

Daily Activities and Adaptations

  • Dressing — Put the affected arm into sleeves first; use front-fastening clothes; try a dressing stick or long-handled shoe horn
  • Reaching — Use a grabber/reacher for high shelves; reorganise cupboards to keep frequently used items at waist to shoulder height
  • Sleeping — Try sleeping on your back with a pillow under the affected arm, or on the unaffected side with a pillow hugging the affected arm
  • Driving — Adjust your seat and mirrors to minimise reaching; consider a steering wheel cover for easier grip

When to Seek Further Help

See your GP if shoulder pain is severe or worsening despite exercises, you have sudden inability to lift your arm (possible rotator cuff tear), you experience numbness or tingling down the arm, or shoulder pain is disrupting sleep consistently. Your GP can refer you to NHS physiotherapy (typically 4–8 weeks wait) or an orthopaedic specialist if needed. Treatments may include corticosteroid injections, hyaluronic acid injections or, in severe cases, shoulder replacement surgery.

Consistent, gentle exercise is the single most effective long-term treatment for shoulder arthritis. Start slowly, be patient with progress and celebrate small improvements. Our virtual assistant can help you create a personalised shoulder exercise programme.

This article is for general information only. Consult a physiotherapist or GP before starting exercises if you have severe shoulder pain or have had recent surgery.

Shoulder Exercises for Osteoarthritis

For shoulder (glenohumeral) osteoarthritis, the priority is restoring pain-free range of motion before adding load. Pendulum swings, wall slides and supine external rotation with a light band are the safest starting points. See our osteoarthritis exercises guide and osteoarthritis treatment overview.

Shoulder Exercises for Rheumatoid Arthritis

Shoulder RA responds best to a low-load, high-repetition approach. During flares, restrict to pendulums and supported range of motion only. Resume strengthening when the joint is no longer warm. See rheumatoid arthritis exercises.

Gentle Shoulder Exercises for Severe Arthritis

Pendulum swings, supported table slides, gentle scapular squeezes and warm-water exercise allow you to keep the shoulder moving without overloading the joint. Two short 10-minute daily sessions are usually better tolerated than one longer one.

Shoulder Exercises After Replacement

After shoulder replacement (anatomic or reverse), follow your surgeon's protocol precisely for the first 6–12 weeks. The strengthening routine on this page typically becomes appropriate beyond 12 weeks, once cleared by your surgical team.

Exercises to Avoid With Shoulder Arthritis

Avoid behind-the-neck lat pulldowns, military presses, upright rows, heavy bench press and any overhead lifting with poor technique. Replace with band external rotation, wall push-ups and seated rows. For a personalised plan, find a shoulder physiotherapist near you.

Shoulder Arthritis Exercise FAQ — People Also Ask

What are the best exercises for arthritic shoulders?

The best routine combines pendulum swings and wall slides (mobility), band external rotation and scapular squeezes (strength), and warm-up with a heat pack for 10 minutes. Done 3–4 times per week, this combination reduces pain and improves overhead reach.

How often should I do shoulder exercises for arthritis?

Mobility daily (5–10 minutes), strengthening 2–3 times per week. Allow at least one rest day between strengthening sessions.

Can exercise cure shoulder arthritis?

No — exercise cannot reverse cartilage loss, but it is the most effective non-surgical treatment and can delay the need for shoulder replacement. Benefits stop if exercise stops.

What shoulder exercises should I avoid with arthritis?

Avoid behind-the-neck lat pulldowns, military presses, upright rows and heavy overhead lifting. Replace with band external rotation, wall push-ups and seated rows.

Are there gentle shoulder exercises for severe arthritis?

Yes — pendulum swings, supported table slides, scapular squeezes and warm-water exercise. Two short 10-minute daily sessions are usually better tolerated.

How long until shoulder exercises reduce arthritis pain?

Reduced stiffness within 2–3 weeks, meaningful pain reduction at 6–8 weeks, full benefit at 12 weeks of consistent practice.

title: Foot and Ankle Arthritis UK: Symptoms, Exercises and Footwear
excerpt: Foot and ankle arthritis symptoms vary by type but commonly include pain, stiffness, and swelling. For big toe arthritis, you might notice difficulty walking.
content:
Your feet contain 33 joints each, making them particularly vulnerable to arthritis. Foot and ankle arthritis affects millions of people across the UK, causing pain with every step and significantly impacting mobility and quality of life. Whether you have osteoarthritis in the big toe, rheumatoid arthritis affecting multiple foot joints, or post-traumatic arthritis following an ankle injury, understanding your condition and knowing the right management strategies can make an enormous difference. This guide covers symptoms, exercises, footwear choices and NHS treatment pathways.

Quick answer: Foot and ankle arthritis symptoms vary by type but commonly include pain, stiffness, and swelling. For big toe arthritis, you might notice difficulty walking and a bony bump. Ankle arthritis often causes deep pain, stiffness in the morning, and swelling. Rheumatoid arthritis in the feet can lead to pain under the ball of the foot and toe deformities, affecting up to 90% of those with RA.

Common Types of Foot Arthritis

Big Toe Arthritis (Hallux Rigidus)

The most common site for foot osteoarthritis. The big toe joint becomes stiff and painful, particularly when pushing off during walking. You may notice a bony bump on top of the joint and difficulty wearing certain shoes. It affects approximately 2.5% of people over 50 in the UK.

Midfoot Arthritis

Affects the joints in the middle of the foot, causing a deep aching pain across the top of the foot that worsens with walking on uneven surfaces. Often develops after previous injury or gradually with age.

Ankle Arthritis

Less common than knee or hip arthritis but can be severely disabling. Most ankle arthritis is post-traumatic — following previous fractures, severe sprains or ligament injuries. Symptoms include deep ankle pain, stiffness (especially in the morning), swelling and difficulty on uneven ground.

Rheumatoid Arthritis of the Feet

RA frequently affects the feet — up to 90% of RA patients develop foot problems during their disease course. RA typically affects the small joints of the toes (metatarsophalangeal joints), causing pain under the ball of the foot, toe deformities (hammer toes, claw toes) and difficulty finding comfortable footwear.

Exercises for Foot and Ankle Arthritis

Regular exercises help maintain mobility, strengthen supporting muscles and reduce stiffness. Perform these daily, ideally after warming your feet (warm footbath for 10 minutes).

Range-of-Motion Exercises

  • Ankle circles — Sit with your foot off the floor. Slowly rotate your ankle in circles, 10 times clockwise, 10 times anticlockwise
  • Toe spreads — Place your foot flat on the floor. Try to spread all toes apart, hold 5 seconds, then relax. Repeat 10 times
  • Toe curls — Place a small towel on the floor. Use your toes to scrunch the towel towards you. This strengthens intrinsic foot muscles
  • Alphabet writing — Lift your foot and use your big toe to "write" the alphabet in the air. This moves the ankle through its full range

Strengthening Exercises

  • Calf raises — Stand holding a chair for balance. Rise onto your toes, hold 3 seconds, then slowly lower. Start with 10 repetitions and build up
  • Resistance band dorsiflexion — Sit with legs extended, loop a resistance band around the ball of your foot. Pull your toes towards you against the band's resistance. 2 sets of 15
  • Marble pick-ups — Place marbles on the floor and pick them up with your toes, placing them in a bowl. Excellent for toe dexterity and strength

Balance Exercises

  • Single-leg stance — Stand near a wall for safety. Lift one foot and balance on the other for 30 seconds. Progress to doing this with eyes closed
  • Tandem walking — Walk heel-to-toe in a straight line, like walking on a tightrope. 10 steps forward and back

Footwear Guide for Foot Arthritis

Choosing the right shoes is one of the most important decisions you can make for arthritic feet. Key features to look for:

  • Wide, deep toe box — Allows room for swollen or deformed toes without pressure
  • Firm heel counter — Supports the heel and reduces excess motion
  • Cushioned sole — Absorbs impact and reduces pressure on painful joints
  • Stiff or rocker sole — For big toe arthritis, a stiff-soled shoe with a rocker bottom reduces the bending required at the big toe joint during walking
  • Removable insole — Allows space for custom orthotics
  • Adjustable fastenings — Velcro or laces accommodate swelling that varies throughout the day
  • Low heel — No more than 2.5 cm (1 inch). High heels increase forefoot pressure dramatically

Recommended UK Brands

  • DB Shoes — Made in Northamptonshire, specialist extra-wide and depth footwear
  • Cosyfeet — UK company specialising in extra-roomy footwear
  • Hotter — Wide-fitting comfort shoes made in the UK
  • New Balance — Available in multiple widths with excellent cushioning
  • Skechers — Memory foam insoles and roomy fits at accessible prices

Orthotics and Insoles

Custom orthotics prescribed by an NHS podiatrist can redistribute pressure away from painful joints, correct biomechanical issues and significantly reduce foot pain. Ask your GP for a podiatry referral — NHS podiatry services are free. Over-the-counter insoles (Superfeet, Scholl) can provide interim relief.

NHS Treatment Pathway

  • GP — Initial assessment, X-rays, blood tests (to check for RA), referral to podiatry or orthopaedics
  • Podiatry — Biomechanical assessment, custom orthotics, nail care, footwear advice
  • Physiotherapy — Exercise programmes, manual therapy, ultrasound treatment
  • Orthopaedics — Steroid injections, surgical options (joint fusion, joint replacement, toe correction)
  • Rheumatology — If inflammatory arthritis is suspected (RA, PsA)

Don't ignore foot pain — it affects your mobility, balance and overall quality of life. Early treatment and the right footwear can make a huge difference. Our virtual assistant can help you find UK podiatry services and footwear options for your specific needs.

This article is for general information only. See your GP or podiatrist for persistent foot pain, especially if you notice swelling, redness or deformity.

Practical next steps for Foot and Ankle Arthritis UK: Symptoms, Exercises and Footwear

If you came here about Foot and Ankle Arthritis UK: Symptoms, Exercises and Footwear, pick one change you can keep for a fortnight rather than overhauling everything at once. Note what hurts, what helps, and what you have already tried, then take that list to your GP, rheumatology nurse or physiotherapist so the conversation stays concrete.

In many areas you can ask your local integrated care board about self-referral to physiotherapy or lifestyle support without waiting for a hospital letter. Check your GP surgery website or the NHS App for the route that applies where you live.

Building a joint-friendly routine

Start with short sessions you can repeat on most days. Warm water, cycling, or paced walking often suits stiff joints better than sudden high-impact bursts. Increase time or resistance slowly, and leave a rest day when a joint is hot, swollen or unusually painful. If you are unsure where to begin, ask about NHS physiotherapy or an exercise referral scheme via your GP surgery.

Pacing on good and bad days

On better days it is tempting to catch up on everything at once. Spread chores and exercise across the week instead. Use the two-hour rule many physiotherapists suggest: if pain or fatigue is clearly worse two hours after activity, the dose was too high — trim the next session rather than stopping altogether.

Making information usable

Treat articles like this as a starting map, not a personal care plan. Highlight one idea to try for two weeks, then review. If symptoms are new, rapidly worsening, or affecting several joints with fever or unexplained weight loss, contact your GP promptly rather than waiting on self-help alone.

Quick questions about Foot Ankle Arthritis Symptoms

Is this a substitute for seeing a clinician? No. Use it to prepare questions and understand options, then confirm decisions with your NHS team.

How long before I judge whether a change helped? Give most habit or exercise changes at least two to four weeks, unless pain or swelling clearly worsens — in that case scale back sooner.

What should I track? Joint pain (0–10), morning stiffness time, sleep quality, and how far you can walk or how long you can type or stand. Patterns beat one-off ratings.

Safety and when to get urgent help

This page is general information for people in the United Kingdom, not personal medical advice. Seek urgent help via NHS 111 or A&E if you have sudden inability to move a joint, hot swollen joint with fever, chest pain, severe shortness of breath, or symptoms that feel immediately dangerous.

title: Hip Replacement for Arthritis – UK Guide
excerpt: Considering a hip replacement for arthritis? UK guide to NHS eligibility, types of hip replacement, recovery timeline, and physiotherapy after surgery.
content:
Around 90,000 hip replacements are performed annually in the UK. It is one of the most reliable operations for relieving arthritis pain, with over 90% of patients reporting excellent results lasting 15-25+ years.

Quick answer: Hip replacement is recommended when severe hip pain impacts daily life and non-surgical treatments have failed. Over 90% of patients experience excellent results lasting 15-25+ years. There are two main types: total hip replacement and hip resurfacing. Recovery typically involves using crutches for 6 weeks, with full benefits usually seen after 12 months, alongside following specific hip precautions.

When Is Hip Replacement Recommended?

  • Severe hip pain affecting sleep, walking, and quality of life
  • Non-surgical treatments have been exhausted (physiotherapy, injections, weight management)
  • X-rays show significant joint damage
  • Difficulty with daily tasks like putting on shoes, climbing stairs, or getting in and out of a car

Types of Hip Replacement

  • Total hip replacement (THR) — both ball and socket are replaced. Most common.
  • Hip resurfacing — the bone is trimmed and capped rather than removed. Less common, sometimes offered to younger patients.
  • Anterior approach — newer technique through the front of the hip. Potentially faster recovery but not available everywhere.

The NHS Process

  1. GP referral to orthopaedic surgeon
  2. Consultation and X-rays
  3. Pre-operative assessment (blood tests, general health check)
  4. Surgery — usually 1-2 hours under spinal anaesthetic
  5. Hospital stay — typically 1-3 days
  6. Follow-up at 6 weeks and 1 year

Recovery Timeline

  • Day 1 — you'll be helped to stand and take steps with a frame
  • Weeks 1-6 — walking with crutches, following hip precautions
  • Week 6 — most people can start driving (if automatic car)
  • Weeks 6-12 — increasing activity, many return to work (desk jobs)
  • 3-6 months — significant improvement, most restrictions lifted
  • 12 months — full benefit usually achieved

Hip Precautions

After surgery, you'll need to follow precautions to prevent dislocation:

  • Don't cross your legs
  • Don't bend your hip past 90 degrees
  • Don't twist your leg inward
  • Use a raised toilet seat and shower seat
  • Sleep on your back or non-operated side with a pillow between your knees

Preparing Your Home

  • Remove trip hazards (loose rugs, trailing cables)
  • Arrange a bed on the ground floor if possible
  • Stock up on easy-to-prepare meals
  • Install grab rails in the bathroom
  • Arrange help for the first 2-3 weeks after surgery

Hip replacement is a life-changing operation for many people with arthritis. Discuss all your options with your surgeon and commit to physiotherapy for the best possible outcome.

Preparing for appointments

Write three priorities before you go: main symptom, functional limit (stairs, sleep, work), and the question you most need answered. Bring a current medicine list including over-the-counter products. If English is not your first language, request an interpreter when you book.

Reliable UK sources

Cross-check major decisions with NHS.uk, your clinical team, and NICE guidance summaries where relevant. Be wary of social posts that promise reversal of arthritis or attack standard medicines without evidence.

title: Anti-Inflammatory Herbs and Spices for Arthritis: A Complete Guide
excerpt: Evidence-based guide to anti-inflammatory herbs and spices for arthritis. Learn about ginger, cinnamon, garlic, rosemary and other natural remedies available.
content:
For centuries, herbs and spices have been used to treat pain and inflammation. Modern science is now validating many of these traditional remedies, identifying the specific compounds responsible for their anti-inflammatory effects and testing them in clinical trials. While no herb or spice can replace medical treatment for arthritis, several have genuine evidence supporting their use as complementary approaches. This guide examines the most promising options available in UK shops and supermarkets.

Quick answer: Several herbs and spices available in UK shops have genuine anti-inflammatory evidence for arthritis, including turmeric (curcumin), ginger, garlic, cinnamon, rosemary and boswellia. None replace medical treatment, but the strongest data are for curcumin at around 1,000 mg/day with an absorption aid, and ginger extract at 500–1,000 mg/day. Use consistently for 4–12 weeks before judging effect.

Ginger (Zingiber officinale)

The Evidence

Ginger is one of the most extensively studied anti-inflammatory spices for arthritis. Its active compounds — gingerols, shogaols and paradols — inhibit the same inflammatory pathways (COX-2, LOX, NF-κB) targeted by conventional anti-inflammatory medications. A meta-analysis of five randomised controlled trials found that ginger significantly reduced pain and disability in osteoarthritis, with effects comparable to ibuprofen in some studies. The evidence is strongest for knee osteoarthritis.

How to Use

  • Fresh ginger — Grate 1–2 cm into stir-fries, soups, smoothies or hot water for ginger tea
  • Ground ginger — ½–1 teaspoon daily added to cooking, porridge or warm drinks
  • Supplements — 500–1,000 mg daily of ginger extract (available from Holland & Barrett, Boots)
  • Ginger tea — Steep fresh sliced ginger in boiling water for 10 minutes. Add honey and lemon

Safety

Generally very safe. May cause mild heartburn in some people. Can interact with blood-thinning medications (warfarin) — check with your GP. Not recommended in doses exceeding 4g daily.

Cinnamon (Cinnamomum)

The Evidence

Cinnamon contains cinnamaldehyde and proanthocyanidins, which have demonstrated anti-inflammatory effects in laboratory studies. A systematic review found cinnamon supplementation reduced inflammatory markers (CRP) in people with metabolic conditions. Limited but promising research specifically in arthritis suggests potential benefits for reducing joint inflammation and oxidative stress.

How to Use

  • Sprinkle on porridge, yoghurt, smoothies or baked fruit
  • Add to warm milk or coffee (golden milk with turmeric and cinnamon is popular)
  • Use Ceylon cinnamon ("true cinnamon") rather than cassia cinnamon, as cassia contains higher levels of coumarin which can affect the liver in large amounts
  • 1–3g daily is commonly used

Garlic (Allium sativum)

The Evidence

Garlic contains diallyl disulphide (DADS), a compound that limits cartilage-damaging enzymes in laboratory studies. A large epidemiological study published in BMC Musculoskeletal Disorders found that women who consumed more garlic had significantly lower rates of hip osteoarthritis. While clinical trial evidence specifically for arthritis pain is limited, garlic's anti-inflammatory properties are well documented.

How to Use

  • Use 1–2 fresh cloves daily in cooking — crush or chop and let stand for 10 minutes before cooking to maximise allicin production
  • Raw garlic is most potent but harder to tolerate — roasted garlic is milder and still beneficial
  • Aged garlic extract supplements are available for those who dislike the taste

Rosemary (Rosmarinus officinalis)

The Evidence

Rosemary contains rosmarinic acid and carnosic acid, both potent antioxidants with anti-inflammatory properties. Laboratory studies show these compounds inhibit COX-2 and reduce inflammatory cytokines. While clinical trial evidence in arthritis is still emerging, the anti-inflammatory mechanisms are well characterised.

How to Use

  • Add fresh or dried rosemary liberally to roasted vegetables, meats and soups
  • Make rosemary tea by steeping a sprig in hot water for 5–10 minutes
  • Rosemary oil can be used topically (diluted in a carrier oil) for joint massage

Green Tea (Camellia sinensis)

The Evidence

Green tea contains epigallocatechin-3-gallate (EGCG), a powerful anti-inflammatory polyphenol. Research published in Arthritis Research & Therapy found EGCG reduced inflammation and cartilage destruction in laboratory models of arthritis. Epidemiological studies suggest regular green tea consumption is associated with lower rates of arthritis and reduced inflammatory markers.

How to Use

  • Drink 2–3 cups of green tea daily — brew at 70–80°C (not boiling) for 2–3 minutes
  • Matcha provides concentrated EGCG
  • Green tea supplements are available but may interact with some medications

Black Pepper (Piper nigrum)

The Evidence

Piperine, the active compound in black pepper, has anti-inflammatory properties and — crucially — dramatically improves the absorption of curcumin from turmeric (by up to 2,000%). It also enhances the bioavailability of other beneficial compounds. Always combine turmeric with black pepper for maximum benefit.

Combining Herbs and Spices

A practical approach to incorporating anti-inflammatory herbs and spices into your daily routine:

  • Morning — Golden milk (warm milk with ½ tsp turmeric, pinch of black pepper, ½ tsp cinnamon, ½ tsp ginger)
  • Lunch — Add fresh garlic and rosemary to soups or salads
  • Afternoon — Green tea
  • Dinner — Cook with ginger, garlic and plenty of herbs and spices

While individual spices may have modest effects, the cumulative benefit of an overall anti-inflammatory dietary pattern — rich in herbs, spices, fruits, vegetables and whole grains — is well supported by evidence. Our virtual assistant can help you plan anti-inflammatory meals using these ingredients.

This article is for general information only. Herbs and spices complement but do not replace medical treatment. Consult your GP before taking herbal supplements, particularly if you take prescription medications.

title: Staying Active with Arthritis in Winter: UK Guide to Cold-Weather Exercise
excerpt: How to stay active with arthritis during UK winters. Indoor exercise ideas, layering tips, warm-up routines and motivation strategies for cold weather joint pain.
content:
Winter in the UK presents a particular challenge for the millions of people living with arthritis. Shorter days, cold temperatures, icy conditions and the natural inclination to hibernate on the sofa can cause physical activity levels to plummet — yet staying active during winter is arguably more important than at any other time of year. Regular movement keeps joints lubricated, muscles strong, weight in check and mood elevated. This guide provides practical strategies for maintaining an active lifestyle throughout the British winter.

Quick answer: In winter, all adults in the UK should take a daily 10-microgram (400 IU) vitamin D supplement, as recommended by Public Health England. This is because between October and March, the UK does not receive enough sunlight for the body to produce sufficient vitamin D, which is vital for bone health, immune function, and may help reduce arthritis inflammation.

Why Winter Activity Matters More

The temptation to rest during cold weather is understandable, but inactivity creates a vicious cycle: less movement leads to stiffer joints, weaker muscles, weight gain and lower mood — all of which worsen arthritis symptoms. Research shows that physical activity levels in the UK drop by 20–30% during winter months, and this decline is even more pronounced among people with chronic pain conditions.

Conversely, maintaining activity through winter helps keep synovial fluid flowing (the joint's natural lubricant), prevent deconditioning and muscle loss, support mental health (combating seasonal affective disorder), maintain a healthy weight through the calorie-dense festive season, and reduce the severity and duration of morning stiffness.

Indoor Exercise Options

When outdoor conditions are poor, having indoor alternatives is essential.

Swimming and Aquatic Exercise

Indoor heated pools offer one of the best exercise environments for arthritis in winter. Warm water (typically 28–32°C) soothes joints, provides buoyancy that reduces weight-bearing stress by up to 90%, and allows movement that would be painful on land. Most UK leisure centres have heated indoor pools. Look for "aquafit" or "gentle aqua" classes specifically suited to people with joint conditions.

Home-Based Exercises

  • Chair-based exercises — Full-body workout from the comfort of your living room. NHS and Versus Arthritis have free YouTube videos
  • Yoga and tai chi — Online classes allow you to practice in a warm home environment
  • Resistance band exercises — Compact, affordable equipment for strength training at home
  • Stationary cycling — Pedal exercisers (from £20) sit on the floor and can be used from a chair
  • Stair exercises — If you have stairs, gentle step-ups using the bottom step provide excellent leg strengthening

Indoor Walking

  • Shopping centres — many open early for "mall walking" groups
  • Indoor athletics tracks (some leisure centres have these)
  • Walking on the spot or marching in place while watching television
  • Indoor walking videos on YouTube (Leslie Sansone's "Walk at Home" series is popular)

Exercising Outdoors Safely

If you prefer outdoor exercise, preparation is key:

Layering for Arthritis

  • Base layer — Moisture-wicking thermal underwear keeps skin dry
  • Middle layer — Fleece or wool for insulation
  • Outer layer — Windproof and waterproof jacket
  • Extremities — Thermal gloves (or arthritis compression gloves under warm gloves), warm hat, thermal socks. Heat loss through the head and hands significantly affects comfort
  • Hand warmers — Reusable gel hand warmers (£2–£5) or disposable warmers can be placed in gloves or pockets

Safety on Ice and Wet Surfaces

  • Wear shoes with good grip — look for deep treads and slip-resistant soles
  • Use walking poles for stability on icy paths
  • Walk on gritted surfaces where possible
  • Take smaller steps to maintain balance
  • Avoid walking after dark when ice is hard to see
  • Slip-on ice grippers for shoes (£5–£15 from outdoor shops) provide extra traction

Warming Up in Cold Weather

Cold muscles and joints need a longer warm-up in winter. Spend 10–15 minutes warming up indoors before heading out: march on the spot, do gentle arm circles, knee lifts and ankle rolls. This increases blood flow to muscles and synovial fluid production before exposing joints to cold temperatures.

Motivation Strategies

  • Schedule exercise — Treat it as an appointment you can't cancel
  • Exercise buddy — Accountability makes you more likely to show up, especially on cold, dark days
  • Midday exercise — Take advantage of daylight during lunch breaks. Even 15 minutes of walking at lunchtime helps
  • Track your activity — Use a simple diary or step counter. Seeing progress is motivating
  • Set winter-specific goals — Rather than comparing to summer activity levels, set realistic winter targets
  • Reward yourself — Plan something enjoyable after exercise: a warm bath, hot chocolate, favourite TV programme
  • Remember the benefits — Exercise improves mood within minutes, and the effects last hours. On the coldest, darkest days, you'll feel the benefit most

Vitamin D in Winter

Between October and March, the UK doesn't receive enough UVB sunlight for vitamin D production. Public Health England recommends all adults take a 10-microgram (400 IU) vitamin D supplement daily during autumn and winter. Vitamin D is important for bone health, immune function and may help reduce arthritis-related inflammation.

Winter doesn't have to mean retreating from physical activity. With the right preparation, indoor alternatives and motivation strategies, you can stay active throughout the British winter and emerge in spring with stronger, more mobile joints. Our virtual assistant can help you create a winter exercise plan tailored to your abilities.

This article is for general information only. Consult your GP before starting a new exercise programme, particularly if you have balance problems or cardiovascular conditions.

Pacing on good and bad days

On better days it is tempting to catch up on everything at once. Spread chores and exercise across the week instead. Use the two-hour rule many physiotherapists suggest: if pain or fatigue is clearly worse two hours after activity, the dose was too high — trim the next session rather than stopping altogether.

Building a joint-friendly routine

Start with short sessions you can repeat on most days. Warm water, cycling, or paced walking often suits stiff joints better than sudden high-impact bursts. Increase time or resistance slowly, and leave a rest day when a joint is hot, swollen or unusually painful. If you are unsure where to begin, ask about NHS physiotherapy or an exercise referral scheme via your GP surgery.

Peer support etiquette

Share what helps you without prescribing it for others. Conditions, medicines and life circumstances differ. If someone is in crisis, encourage them toward NHS 111, their GP, or emergency services rather than relying on a forum alone.

title: TENS Machines for Arthritis UK: Do They Work and How to Use Them
excerpt: Complete UK guide to using TENS machines for arthritis pain. How they work, evidence for effectiveness, best devices, settings and NHS availability.
content:
TENS (Transcutaneous Electrical Nerve Stimulation) machines are one of the most popular drug-free pain relief options for arthritis in the UK. These small, battery-powered devices deliver mild electrical impulses through electrode pads placed on the skin near painful joints. With prices starting from just £15 and no prescription needed, TENS machines are accessible and widely used — but do they actually work for arthritis? This guide examines the evidence, explains how to use one effectively and helps you choose the right device.

Quick answer: TENS machines are drug-free devices that deliver mild electrical impulses through pads on the skin, a popular choice for arthritis pain relief. They work by stimulating nerves to "close the gate" on pain signals (high frequency, 80-120 Hz) and by triggering endorphin release (low frequency, 2-5 Hz). Evidence suggests short-term pain relief, but they are best used as part of a wider pain management plan.

How TENS Works

TENS machines work through two main mechanisms:

Gate Control Theory

At high frequencies (80–120 Hz), TENS stimulates large nerve fibres that "close the gate" on pain signals travelling to the brain. Essentially, the tingling sensation from the TENS overrides the pain signals, reducing your perception of pain. This is similar to rubbing a bumped elbow — the pressure sensation partially blocks the pain signal.

Endorphin Release

At lower frequencies (2–5 Hz), TENS triggers the release of endorphins — the body's natural painkillers. This takes longer to work (20–30 minutes) but the pain relief can last longer after the device is switched off.

What the Evidence Says

The evidence for TENS in arthritis is mixed but generally positive for short-term pain relief:

  • A Cochrane review of TENS for knee osteoarthritis found some evidence of pain reduction, though study quality was variable
  • A meta-analysis in Physiotherapy found TENS provided statistically significant pain relief for OA compared to placebo
  • NICE acknowledges TENS as an option for osteoarthritis pain management alongside other treatments
  • Many rheumatology and physiotherapy departments in the UK recommend TENS as part of multimodal pain management
  • Patient satisfaction is generally high — many users report meaningful pain relief even when clinical trial results are modest

TENS is best viewed as one tool in a pain management toolkit, not a standalone treatment. It works well alongside exercise, medication and other approaches.

How to Use a TENS Machine for Arthritis

Pad Placement

Correct electrode placement is crucial for effective pain relief:

  • Knee arthritis — Place two pads on either side of the kneecap, or one above and one below the joint
  • Hip arthritis — Place pads around the hip joint — one at the front, one at the side or back
  • Hand/wrist arthritis — Use smaller pads on either side of the painful joint
  • Shoulder arthritis — Place pads on the front and back of the shoulder, or above and below the joint
  • Spine/back arthritis — Place pads on either side of the spine at the painful level (never directly on the spine)

Settings

  • Start with a high frequency (80–100 Hz) for immediate tingling pain relief
  • Try low frequency (2–5 Hz) for deeper, endorphin-based relief
  • Increase intensity gradually until you feel a strong but comfortable tingling — it should never be painful
  • Use for 20–60 minutes per session, up to several times daily
  • Experiment with settings — what works varies between individuals

Tips for Best Results

  • Clean and dry the skin before applying pads
  • Don't place pads on broken skin, over varicose veins or near the front of the neck
  • Replace electrode pads when they lose stickiness (every 20–30 uses typically)
  • Use during activities that usually cause pain (walking, gardening, housework)
  • Try using TENS before exercise to enable more comfortable movement

Choosing a TENS Machine

Key features to consider:

  • Dual channel — Allows you to use 4 pads simultaneously for larger areas or multiple joints
  • Adjustable frequency and intensity — More control over settings for optimal relief
  • Rechargeable battery — More economical than disposable batteries
  • Pre-set programmes — Useful for beginners, with settings optimised for different pain types
  • Timer — Automatic shut-off prevents overuse

Where to Buy in the UK

  • Boots, Superdrug and Lloyds Pharmacy stock TENS machines (from £15)
  • Amazon and online retailers offer a wide range
  • Physiotherapy suppliers (e.g., TensCare, Beurer) for more advanced devices
  • Some NHS physiotherapy departments loan TENS machines for trial periods — ask your physiotherapist

Who Should Not Use TENS

  • People with pacemakers or other implanted electrical devices (unless approved by cardiologist)
  • During pregnancy (certain pad placements)
  • Over areas of reduced sensation (neuropathy)
  • On active cancer sites
  • While driving or operating machinery

TENS machines are a safe, affordable and drug-free option for arthritis pain relief. While they don't work for everyone, many people find them a valuable addition to their pain management routine. Our virtual assistant can help you with pad placement guidance for your specific joints.

This article is for general information only. Consult your GP or physiotherapist if you're unsure whether TENS is suitable for you.

Keep a short diary of bad days, help you need with dressing or cooking, and walking limits. Welfare rights advisers at local councils or charities can check forms before you submit them.

Work, rights and practical adjustments

Under the Equality Act 2010, employers in Great Britain should consider reasonable adjustments when arthritis has a substantial long-term effect. That can mean flexible hours, more breaks, seating, parking closer to the entrance, or software that reduces typing strain. Acas and Citizens Advice both publish plain-English guides you can take into a meeting.

Preparing for appointments

Write three priorities before you go: main symptom, functional limit (stairs, sleep, work), and the question you most need answered. Bring a current medicine list including over-the-counter products. If English is not your first language, request an interpreter when you book.

Working with NHS pathways

Most people start with GP care, community physiotherapy and self-management, with rheumatology involved when inflammatory disease is suspected or treatment needs escalate. Ask what monitoring blood tests or reviews you should expect, and who to contact between appointments if a flare escalates.

Peer support etiquette

Share what helps you without prescribing it for others. Conditions, medicines and life circumstances differ. If someone is in crisis, encourage them toward NHS 111, their GP, or emergency services rather than relying on a forum alone.

title: Gardening with Arthritis – UK Tips & Adapted Tools
excerpt: Love gardening but struggling with arthritis? UK guide to adapted tools, ergonomic techniques, and ways to enjoy your garden with less joint pain.
content:
Gardening is one of the UK's most popular hobbies, and arthritis shouldn't stop you enjoying it. With the right tools, techniques, and pacing, you can continue gardening safely and comfortably.

Quick answer: Gardening with arthritis is achievable by using adapted tools and techniques. Ergonomic hand tools, long-handled tools, and ratchet secateurs reduce strain. Raised garden beds eliminate bending and kneeling. Pacing yourself by taking breaks, spreading tasks, and alternating positions also helps. Carrying items close to your body and using foam grips on tools are joint-friendly techniques to minimise discomfort.

Benefits of Gardening with Arthritis

  • Gentle exercise that improves joint flexibility and strength
  • Being outdoors boosts mood and reduces stress
  • Vitamin D from sunlight helps bone and joint health
  • Sense of achievement and purpose
  • Growing your own anti-inflammatory foods (turmeric, berries, herbs)

Adapted Gardening Tools

  • Ergonomic hand tools — angled handles reduce wrist strain (Radius Garden, Peta UK)
  • Long-handled tools — reduce bending and kneeling (arm-length trowels, extended hoes)
  • Ratchet secateurs — require 70% less grip force than standard secateurs
  • Kneeling pad with handles — supports getting up and down
  • Garden scooter/seat — wheeled seat for working at ground level
  • Lightweight hosepipe — easier to handle than heavy rubber hoses
  • Electric/battery tools — cordless hedge trimmers, lawn mowers reduce effort

Raised Bed Gardening

Raised beds are the single best adaptation for arthritis gardeners:

  • Eliminate bending and kneeling
  • Can be built at waist or wheelchair height
  • Available as kits from garden centres (from £30)
  • Ideal on patios and small gardens
  • Can grow vegetables, herbs, and flowers

Pacing Your Gardening

  • Limit sessions to 20-30 minutes, then take a break
  • Spread heavy tasks across several days
  • Garden during warmer parts of the day when joints are looser
  • Alternate between standing, kneeling, and sitting tasks
  • Don't try to "finish" in one session — there's always tomorrow

Joint-Friendly Techniques

  • Use your whole body, not just your hands and wrists
  • Carry items close to your body
  • Push wheelbarrows rather than lifting
  • Use a foam grip on tool handles for extra cushioning
  • Wear gardening gloves with padding for joint protection

Where to Buy Adapted Garden Tools in the UK

  • Peta (UK) — specialist adaptive tools (petauk.com)
  • Thrive — charity supporting therapeutic gardening
  • Garden centres — most now stock ergonomic ranges
  • Amazon UK — wide range of adaptive garden equipment

Gardening is excellent therapy for both body and mind. Don't give it up — adapt it to suit your abilities.

title: Spinal Arthritis and Back Pain UK: Symptoms, Treatment and Self-Help
excerpt: UK guide to spinal arthritis and back pain. Understand spondylosis symptoms, NHS diagnosis, exercises for spinal OA and when to see your GP about back stiffness.
content:
Spinal arthritis — medically known as spondylosis — is one of the most common causes of chronic back and neck pain in the UK. Affecting the facet joints, discs and vertebrae of the spine, it's estimated that over 80% of people over 40 show some evidence of spinal degeneration on X-ray, though not all experience symptoms. This guide explains what spinal arthritis is, how it's diagnosed, and provides practical self-help strategies recommended by UK healthcare professionals.

Quick answer: Spinal arthritis, also known as spondylosis, affects the facet joints, discs, and vertebrae of the spine, causing chronic back and neck pain. Symptoms include stiffness, reduced flexibility, and pain that improves with gentle movement. Management involves exercises such as pelvic tilts and chin tucks, maintaining good posture, and sometimes physiotherapy or pain medication. Seek urgent medical attention for loss of bladder/bowel control or sudden weakness.

What Is Spinal Arthritis?

The spine is made up of 33 vertebrae connected by facet joints at the back and intervertebral discs at the front. Spinal arthritis most commonly involves osteoarthritis of the facet joints (facet joint arthropathy) and degeneration of the intervertebral discs (degenerative disc disease). These changes occur naturally with age but can be accelerated by injury, genetics, obesity and occupational factors.

Areas Affected

  • Cervical spine (neck) — Causes neck pain, stiffness and sometimes headaches. May cause nerve compression leading to arm pain, tingling or weakness
  • Thoracic spine (mid-back) — Less commonly affected due to the stabilising effect of the rib cage
  • Lumbar spine (lower back) — The most common area for spinal arthritis, causing lower back pain, stiffness and sometimes leg symptoms (sciatica)

Symptoms

  • Stiffness and pain in the back or neck, worse in the morning and after inactivity
  • Pain that improves with gentle movement but worsens with prolonged standing or walking
  • Reduced flexibility — difficulty bending, twisting or looking over your shoulder
  • Grinding or crunching sensation (crepitus) with movement
  • Pain that radiates into the buttocks, hips or legs (lumbar) or shoulders and arms (cervical)
  • Numbness, tingling or weakness in limbs (if nerves are compressed — seek medical attention)

Exercises for Spinal Arthritis

Exercise is the cornerstone of spinal arthritis management. These exercises should be performed daily:

Lower Back

  • Pelvic tilts — Lie on your back with knees bent. Gently flatten your lower back against the floor by tightening your abdominal muscles. Hold 5 seconds, release. Repeat 15 times
  • Knee rolls — Lie on your back with knees bent. Slowly roll both knees to one side, keeping shoulders flat. Hold 10 seconds, then roll to the other side. Repeat 10 times each side
  • Cat-cow stretch — On hands and knees, slowly arch your back upward (cat), then dip it downward (cow). Move gently between positions 10 times
  • Bridge — Lie on your back, knees bent. Lift your hips off the floor until your body forms a straight line from shoulders to knees. Hold 5 seconds. Repeat 10 times

Neck

  • Chin tucks — Sit with good posture. Draw your chin straight back (creating a "double chin"). Hold 5 seconds. This strengthens deep neck flexors. Repeat 10 times
  • Gentle neck rotations — Slowly turn your head to look over each shoulder. Hold 5 seconds each side. Repeat 5 times
  • Neck side bends — Tilt your ear towards your shoulder (don't raise the shoulder). Hold 10 seconds each side

Core Strengthening

A strong core supports the spine and reduces load on arthritic joints:

  • Dead bug — Lie on your back, arms pointing to the ceiling, knees bent at 90°. Slowly extend one arm overhead while extending the opposite leg. Return and switch sides. 2 sets of 10
  • Side plank (modified) — Lie on your side, propped on your elbow, knees bent. Lift your hips off the floor. Hold 10–20 seconds. This targets the obliques that stabilise the spine

Posture and Ergonomics

  • Sit with your back supported — use a lumbar roll or rolled towel in the curve of your lower back
  • Adjust your computer screen to eye level to avoid sustained neck flexion
  • Take movement breaks every 30 minutes — prolonged sitting increases spinal stiffness
  • Sleep on a supportive mattress — medium-firm is generally recommended. Place a pillow between your knees when side-sleeping
  • Lift objects by bending your knees and keeping the load close to your body

NHS Treatment Options

  • Physiotherapy — Tailored exercise programmes, manual therapy and education. Available through GP referral
  • Pain medication — Paracetamol, NSAIDs (topical and oral), and sometimes neuropathic pain medications for nerve-related symptoms
  • Facet joint injections — Corticosteroid injections into the affected facet joints, performed by pain specialists or radiologists
  • Pain management programmes — Multidisciplinary programmes combining exercise, psychology and education
  • Surgery — Rarely needed. Options include decompression (removing bone pressing on nerves) or spinal fusion in severe cases

When to See Your GP Urgently

Most back pain from spinal arthritis is manageable, but see your GP urgently or attend A&E if you experience loss of bladder or bowel control, numbness in the genital/saddle area, sudden severe weakness in both legs, or worsening numbness/weakness in arms or legs. These symptoms may indicate cauda equina syndrome or cord compression, which require emergency assessment.

Spinal arthritis is extremely common and usually very manageable with regular exercise, good posture habits and appropriate treatment. Our virtual assistant can help you create a tailored back exercise programme.

title: Gut Health and Arthritis: The Microbiome Connection Explained
excerpt: Explore the link between gut health and arthritis. How your microbiome affects joint inflammation, best foods for gut health and practical steps to improve.
content:
One of the most exciting areas of arthritis research in recent years has been the discovery that the trillions of bacteria living in your gut — collectively known as the gut microbiome — play a significant role in inflammation and immune function throughout your entire body, including your joints. This emerging science is reshaping our understanding of why arthritis develops and how dietary changes might help manage it. This guide explains the gut-arthritis connection in plain English and provides practical steps you can take today.

Quick answer: The gut microbiome, comprising trillions of bacteria, significantly influences inflammation and immune function crucial for arthritis. An imbalance in gut bacteria, known as dysbiosis, may trigger or worsen autoimmune responses. Increased intestinal permeability ("leaky gut") allows bacterial fragments into the bloodstream, causing widespread inflammation. Dietary changes, such as consuming prebiotic and probiotic foods, can support a diverse and healthy gut microbiome.

What Is the Gut Microbiome?

Your gut contains approximately 100 trillion microorganisms — bacteria, fungi, viruses and other microbes — collectively weighing about 2 kg. This community of microbes, predominantly in the large intestine, is unique to each individual and influenced by diet, medications, lifestyle and environment. A healthy microbiome contains a diverse range of beneficial bacteria that aid digestion, produce vitamins, train the immune system and help regulate inflammation throughout the body.

How Gut Health Affects Arthritis

The Immune System Connection

Approximately 70% of your immune system resides in or around the gut. The gut-associated lymphoid tissue (GALT) is the largest immune organ in the body. Gut bacteria directly influence how the immune system develops and functions. In inflammatory arthritis (RA, PsA), the immune system mistakenly attacks joints — and there's growing evidence that imbalances in gut bacteria (dysbiosis) may trigger or perpetuate this autoimmune response.

Intestinal Permeability ("Leaky Gut")

When the gut barrier becomes more permeable than normal, bacterial fragments and other molecules can cross into the bloodstream, triggering widespread immune activation and inflammation. Research has found increased intestinal permeability in people with rheumatoid arthritis, ankylosing spondylitis and psoriatic arthritis. While "leaky gut" is sometimes overhyped in alternative health circles, the underlying science of intestinal permeability and its role in autoimmunity is legitimate and actively researched.

Specific Bacterial Links

  • Studies have found that people with RA have different gut bacterial profiles compared to healthy individuals — notably reduced diversity and specific bacterial imbalances
  • The bacterium Prevotella copri has been found in higher levels in people with new-onset RA
  • Reduced levels of beneficial bacteria (particularly Bifidobacterium and Bacteroides) have been observed in RA patients
  • The gut microbiome of people with psoriatic arthritis shows characteristic alterations that overlap with patterns seen in psoriasis and inflammatory bowel disease

Osteoarthritis Too

Even osteoarthritis — traditionally viewed as a "wear and tear" condition — has a gut connection. Research from the University of Rochester found that an unhealthy gut microbiome (induced by a high-fat diet in animal studies) accelerated OA progression. The mechanism involves systemic low-grade inflammation driven by gut bacterial products entering the bloodstream. Obesity-related OA may partly work through this gut-inflammation pathway.

Foods That Support Gut Health

Prebiotic Foods (Feed Good Bacteria)

  • Vegetables — Onions, garlic, leeks, asparagus, artichokes, chicory root
  • Fruits — Bananas (especially slightly underripe), apples, berries
  • Whole grains — Oats, barley, rye bread
  • Legumes — Lentils, chickpeas, beans
  • Nuts and seeds — Almonds, flaxseeds

Probiotic Foods (Contain Live Beneficial Bacteria)

  • Live yoghurt — Look for "live cultures" on the label. Available in every UK supermarket
  • Kefir — A fermented milk drink increasingly available in UK shops (Biotiful, Yeo Valley)
  • Sauerkraut — Unpasteurised, from the chilled section (pasteurised versions have no live bacteria)
  • Kimchi — Fermented Korean vegetables, available in most UK supermarkets
  • Kombucha — Fermented tea, widely available in the UK
  • Miso — Fermented soybean paste, excellent in soups

Polyphenol-Rich Foods

Polyphenols are plant compounds that beneficial gut bacteria thrive on: dark chocolate (70%+ cocoa), green tea, berries, red grapes, extra-virgin olive oil, red onions and herbs/spices.

Foods That May Harm Gut Health

  • Ultra-processed foods — Emulsifiers, artificial sweeteners and additives may damage the gut barrier
  • Excessive sugar — Feeds less beneficial bacteria and reduces diversity
  • Excessive alcohol — Damages the gut lining and disrupts bacterial balance
  • Unnecessary antibiotics — Can devastate beneficial bacteria (always take when prescribed, but don't request for viral infections)

Probiotic Supplements

The evidence for probiotic supplements in arthritis is still developing:

  • Several small studies have shown modest benefits of specific probiotic strains for RA symptoms
  • A meta-analysis found probiotic supplementation reduced inflammatory markers (CRP) in RA patients
  • The most studied strains for inflammation include Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium species
  • Evidence is promising but not yet strong enough for formal clinical recommendations
  • If you try a probiotic, choose a reputable brand with specific named strains and use for at least 4 weeks

Practical Steps

  1. Eat 30 different plants per week — Diversity is the single most important factor for a healthy microbiome. Count vegetables, fruits, nuts, seeds, grains, legumes and herbs
  2. Include a fermented food daily — Live yoghurt, kefir, sauerkraut or kimchi
  3. Eat more fibre — Most UK adults eat only 18g/day; the target is 30g. Increase gradually to avoid bloating
  4. Reduce ultra-processed food — Cook from scratch when possible
  5. Stay hydrated — Water supports gut function
  6. Exercise regularly — Physical activity independently improves microbiome diversity

The gut-arthritis connection is a rapidly evolving field with genuine potential to improve arthritis management. While we're still learning the details, the dietary steps above will support both gut health and overall well-being. Our virtual assistant can help you plan gut-friendly meals.

This article is for general information only. The gut microbiome is a complex area of active research. Consult your GP before making major dietary changes or starting supplements.

Food-first is usually safer than stacking capsules. If you do try a supplement, choose a reputable UK brand, check for interactions with your medicines (especially blood thinners), and give any trial a clear stop date so you can judge whether symptoms truly changed.

No single food cures arthritis. Patterns rich in vegetables, fruit, pulses, wholegrains and oily fish are the ones most often discussed in UK dietetic advice for inflammatory conditions. Keep changes realistic: swap one ultra-processed snack for fruit and nuts, or cook with olive oil more often than seed oils marketed as miracle cures.

Noticing catastrophic thoughts ("this flare will never end") and reframing them with paced facts can reduce fear without denying real pain. Apps and courses based on cognitive behavioural approaches are available on the NHS in many areas; your surgery can advise what is offered locally.

title: Hydrotherapy for Arthritis UK: Benefits, Access and What to Expect
excerpt: Complete UK guide to hydrotherapy for arthritis. Learn about warm-water therapy benefits, finding NHS hydrotherapy pools, what happens in a session.
content:
Hydrotherapy — exercise in warm water, typically 33–36°C — is one of the most effective and enjoyable treatments for arthritis. The combination of warmth, buoyancy and water resistance creates an ideal exercise environment where joints can move freely with minimal pain. Recommended by NICE, the NHS and Versus Arthritis, hydrotherapy has a strong evidence base for improving pain, stiffness, strength and function in both osteoarthritis and inflammatory arthritis. This guide explains the benefits, helps you access NHS hydrotherapy services and tells you what to expect.

Quick answer: Hydrotherapy is exercising in warm water, typically 33–36°C, helping arthritis by reducing body weight, allowing easier movement. The warmth relaxes muscles and lessens pain, while water resistance builds strength. NHS sessions, usually 30–45 minutes, are led by a physiotherapist, with courses often lasting 6–12 weeks. Access is usually via GP or rheumatologist referral.

How Hydrotherapy Helps Arthritis

Buoyancy

When immersed to waist depth, your body weight is reduced by approximately 50%. At chest depth, weight-bearing stress is reduced by up to 80%. This allows movements that would be painful on land to be performed with significantly less joint loading. People who struggle to walk comfortably on land often find they can walk, squat and exercise freely in water.

Warmth

Hydrotherapy pools are heated to 33–36°C (compared to standard swimming pools at 26–28°C). This warmth relaxes muscles, increases blood flow to joints, reduces pain perception and improves the elasticity of connective tissues. Many people describe the immediate relief of entering warm water as one of the most pleasant experiences of their arthritis management.

Hydrostatic Pressure

The pressure of water around the body reduces swelling in joints and limbs, provides support during movement, and improves circulation. This is particularly beneficial for people with swollen ankles, knees or hands.

Resistance

Water provides natural resistance to movement — approximately 12 times more resistance than air. This means exercises performed in water provide muscle strengthening without the need for weights or equipment. The resistance is proportional to speed, so you can control the intensity simply by moving faster or slower.

What the Evidence Says

  • A Cochrane review found aquatic exercise significantly improved pain, function and quality of life in knee and hip OA
  • Research published in Physical Therapy found hydrotherapy produced greater improvements in pain and function than land-based exercise for knee OA
  • A systematic review in Rheumatology found that aquatic exercise was beneficial for RA, improving joint tenderness, mood and overall well-being
  • NICE recommends hydrotherapy as part of multimodal management for OA
  • Benefits typically appear within 4–6 weeks of regular sessions

What Happens in a Hydrotherapy Session

A typical NHS hydrotherapy session lasts 30–45 minutes and is led by a physiotherapist or specialist hydrotherapy assistant:

  1. Assessment — Before your first session, a physiotherapist will assess your joints, mobility and goals
  2. Warm-up — Gentle walking and arm movements in the water
  3. Exercises — Tailored exercises targeting your specific joints — may include walking, squats, leg lifts, arm exercises, stretches and balance work
  4. Cool-down — Gentle stretches and relaxation in the warm water

Sessions may be individual (one-to-one with a therapist) or group-based (typically 4–8 people). Group sessions are social and motivating, while individual sessions allow more tailored exercises.

Accessing NHS Hydrotherapy

  • GP referral — Ask your GP to refer you to physiotherapy, specifically requesting hydrotherapy if available locally
  • Direct physiotherapy referral — Many NHS trusts accept self-referrals to physiotherapy
  • Rheumatology team — If you're under a rheumatologist, they can refer directly to hydrotherapy
  • Waiting times — Typically 4–12 weeks, though this varies by area
  • Course length — Usually 6–12 sessions

Finding Hydrotherapy Pools

Dedicated hydrotherapy pools exist at many NHS hospitals, community health centres, some private physiotherapy clinics and charity facilities (Versus Arthritis lists some). Not all areas have easy access — if NHS hydrotherapy is unavailable, many public leisure centres offer "warm water" or "gentle aqua" sessions in pools heated to higher temperatures than standard.

Private Hydrotherapy

Private hydrotherapy sessions typically cost £40–£80 per session. Some private health insurance covers hydrotherapy with a GP or consultant referral. Private sessions usually have shorter waiting times and more flexibility in scheduling.

Swimming vs Hydrotherapy

While both involve water, they differ significantly. Hydrotherapy pools are warmer (33–36°C vs 26–28°C), smaller and shallower with easy access (ramps, hoists). Sessions are supervised and exercises tailored to individual needs. Standard swimming is excellent exercise for arthritis but doesn't provide the same therapeutic warmth. Both are beneficial — hydrotherapy is typically more appropriate for those with severe symptoms, while regular swimming maintains fitness once symptoms are better controlled.

Tips for Getting the Most from Hydrotherapy

  • Continue your exercises at home between sessions — your physiotherapist will give you a home programme
  • Arrive early to shower and change at a relaxed pace
  • Bring a water bottle — you can get dehydrated in warm water without realising
  • Rest afterwards if needed — warm-water exercise can be tiring initially
  • After your NHS course ends, continue with public pool sessions to maintain benefits

Hydrotherapy is one of the most effective and enjoyable treatments available for arthritis. If you haven't tried it, ask your GP about access. Our virtual assistant can help you find hydrotherapy pools and warm-water exercise classes near you.

This article is for general information only. Hydrotherapy may not be suitable if you have certain medical conditions (uncontrolled blood pressure, open wounds, certain infections). Your physiotherapist will assess suitability.

Building a joint-friendly routine

Start with short sessions you can repeat on most days. Warm water, cycling, or paced walking often suits stiff joints better than sudden high-impact bursts. Increase time or resistance slowly, and leave a rest day when a joint is hot, swollen or unusually painful. If you are unsure where to begin, ask about NHS physiotherapy or an exercise referral scheme via your GP surgery.

Pacing on good and bad days

On better days it is tempting to catch up on everything at once. Spread chores and exercise across the week instead. Use the two-hour rule many physiotherapists suggest: if pain or fatigue is clearly worse two hours after activity, the dose was too high — trim the next session rather than stopping altogether.

Work, rights and practical adjustments

Under the Equality Act 2010, employers in Great Britain should consider reasonable adjustments when arthritis has a substantial long-term effect. That can mean flexible hours, more breaks, seating, parking closer to the entrance, or software that reduces typing strain. Acas and Citizens Advice both publish plain-English guides you can take into a meeting.

Benefits conversations

Personal Independence Payment (PIP) looks at how your condition affects daily living and mobility, not the diagnosis name alone. Keep a short diary of bad days, help you need with dressing or cooking, and walking limits. Welfare rights advisers at local councils or charities can check forms before you submit them.

Working with NHS pathways

Most people start with GP care, community physiotherapy and self-management, with rheumatology involved when inflammatory disease is suspected or treatment needs escalate. Ask what monitoring blood tests or reviews you should expect, and who to contact between appointments if a flare escalates.

Preparing for appointments

Write three priorities before you go: main symptom, functional limit (stairs, sleep, work), and the question you most need answered. Bring a current medicine list including over-the-counter products. If English is not your first language, request an interpreter when you book.

How long before I judge whether a change helped? Give most habit or exercise changes at least two to four weeks, unless pain or swelling clearly worsens — in that case scale back sooner.

What should I track? Joint pain (0–10), morning stiffness time, sleep quality, and how far you can walk or how long you can type or stand. Patterns beat one-off ratings.

title: Arthritis and Pet Ownership – UK Guide
excerpt: Can you keep a pet with arthritis? UK guide to the benefits and challenges of pet ownership when living with arthritis, plus practical adaptations.
content:
Pets can bring immense joy, companionship, and even health benefits to people with arthritis. But pet ownership also presents practical challenges when you have limited mobility or painful joints. Here's how to make it work.

Quick answer: Pet ownership can benefit people with arthritis by providing motivation to move, reducing loneliness, distracting from pain, and encouraging routine. Challenges like dog walking, feeding, and grooming can be managed by using adapted equipment, choosing appropriate pets, and utilising services like dog walkers or professional groomers. Organisations such as Cinnamon Trust offer support.

Benefits of Pet Ownership with Arthritis

  • Motivation to move — dog walking ensures regular low-impact exercise
  • Reduced loneliness — companionship reduces social isolation
  • Pain distraction — stroking a pet releases oxytocin and reduces pain perception
  • Routine — pets encourage a structured daily routine
  • Mental health — pet owners report lower rates of depression and anxiety
  • Studies show pet owners with chronic pain use fewer pain medications

Practical Challenges and Solutions

Dog Walking

  • Use a dog walking harness or lead with padded handle to reduce grip strain
  • Choose routes with benches for rest stops
  • Consider a dog walking service on flare days (from £10 per walk in most UK areas)
  • Smaller dogs are easier to manage on lead
  • Look into Cinnamon Trust — a UK charity that helps people with illness walk their dogs

Feeding

  • Raised feeding bowls eliminate bending
  • Use a scoop rather than lifting heavy bags
  • Store food in a container at waist height
  • Automatic feeders for cats can reduce daily effort

Grooming

  • Choose breeds with low grooming needs if getting a new pet
  • Use ergonomic grooming brushes with thick handles
  • Consider professional grooming every 6-8 weeks

Litter Trays (Cats)

  • Self-cleaning litter trays reduce manual scooping
  • Place the tray at a comfortable height
  • Use lightweight clumping litter that's easier to handle

Choosing the Right Pet

  • Low-energy dog breeds — Cavalier King Charles Spaniel, Shih Tzu, Greyhound (surprisingly lazy!)
  • Cats — independent, require less physical management
  • Small pets — rabbits, guinea pigs — lower physical demands
  • Consider an older rescue pet — less energetic, already trained

UK Support Services

  • Cinnamon Trust — volunteers help walk dogs and foster pets if you're hospitalised
  • PDSA — free vet care for eligible pet owners
  • Blue Cross — financial assistance for pet healthcare
  • Dogs for Good — assistance dogs for people with physical disabilities

A pet can be a wonderful companion on your arthritis journey. With the right planning and support, pet ownership is absolutely possible.

title: Arthritis Meal Planning UK: Weekly Menus for Joint Health
excerpt: Practical weekly meal plans for arthritis. Budget-friendly UK recipes following the Mediterranean diet with anti-inflammatory foods to support joint health.
content:
Knowing that an anti-inflammatory diet helps arthritis is one thing — actually planning and preparing meals each week is quite another. This guide provides practical, budget-friendly meal plans specifically designed for people with arthritis in the UK, using ingredients readily available in British supermarkets. Each recipe is designed to be simple, requiring minimal chopping and preparation — because we know that hand and wrist pain can make cooking a challenge.

Quick answer: An arthritis meal plan focuses on anti-inflammatory foods like vegetables, fruits, whole grains, lean protein, and healthy fats. It prioritises Omega-3s, aiming for oily fish twice weekly, and encourages colourful plates for diverse antioxidants. Practical tips include batch cooking, simple preparations to minimise hand strain, and budget-friendly choices like frozen vegetables and tinned fish.

Principles of Arthritis Meal Planning

  • Anti-inflammatory focus — Centre meals around vegetables, fruits, whole grains, lean protein and healthy fats
  • Omega-3 priority — Include oily fish at least twice per week
  • Colourful plates — Different colours represent different antioxidants. Aim for the rainbow
  • Batch cooking — Cook larger portions and freeze in individual servings for difficult days
  • Simple preparation — Minimal chopping, one-pot meals and traybakes reduce hand strain
  • Budget-friendly — Anti-inflammatory eating doesn't need to be expensive. Tinned fish, frozen vegetables, lentils and seasonal produce keep costs down

Sample Week 1: Winter Menu

Monday

  • Breakfast — Overnight oats with frozen berries, walnuts and a drizzle of honey (prepare the night before — no morning effort needed)
  • Lunch — Tinned sardines on wholemeal toast with sliced tomato and a handful of rocket
  • Dinner — One-pot chicken and vegetable stew with sweet potato (simply chop everything into a pot with stock and simmer for 45 minutes)

Tuesday

  • Breakfast — Live yoghurt with a handful of mixed nuts and a sprinkle of cinnamon
  • Lunch — Lentil and vegetable soup (batch cook on Sunday and reheat). Wholemeal bread roll
  • Dinner — Baked salmon fillets with roasted Mediterranean vegetables (courgette, peppers, cherry tomatoes, olive oil — all on one tray, 20 minutes)

Wednesday

  • Breakfast — Porridge with grated fresh ginger, a banana and flaxseeds
  • Lunch — Hummus, roasted vegetable and spinach wholemeal wrap
  • Dinner — Bean and vegetable chilli with brown rice (use tinned beans and passata for ease)

Thursday

  • Breakfast — Scrambled eggs on wholemeal toast with a handful of cherry tomatoes
  • Lunch — Leftover bean chilli (from yesterday) with an avocado side salad
  • Dinner — Grilled mackerel with new potatoes and steamed broccoli drizzled with lemon and olive oil

Friday

  • Breakfast — Anti-inflammatory smoothie (frozen berries, banana, spinach, ginger, turmeric, almond milk)
  • Lunch — Jacket potato with tinned tuna, sweetcorn and a mixed salad
  • Dinner — Chicken stir-fry with ginger, garlic, mixed vegetables and wholemeal noodles

Weekend

  • Saturday — Batch cooking day: prepare a large pot of soup or stew for the freezer. Enjoy a leisurely brunch of smoked salmon, scrambled eggs and avocado on sourdough
  • Sunday — Roast chicken with roasted root vegetables (parsnips, carrots, sweet potato). Use leftovers for Monday's lunch

Quick Anti-Inflammatory Recipes

Golden Turmeric Porridge (5 minutes)

Cook 50g oats with 250ml milk or plant milk. Stir in ½ tsp turmeric, ¼ tsp cinnamon, a pinch of black pepper and 1 tsp honey. Top with walnuts and blueberries. This provides anti-inflammatory turmeric (enhanced by black pepper), omega-3 from walnuts and antioxidants from berries.

One-Tray Mediterranean Salmon (20 minutes)

Place two salmon fillets on a baking tray lined with foil. Surround with halved cherry tomatoes, sliced courgette and pitted olives. Drizzle everything with olive oil, scatter with dried oregano and squeeze over lemon juice. Bake at 200°C for 18–20 minutes. Serve with wholegrain couscous.

Simple Lentil Soup (30 minutes, serves 4)

Sauté a diced onion and 2 crushed garlic cloves in olive oil. Add 200g red lentils, a tin of chopped tomatoes, 1 litre vegetable stock, 1 tsp turmeric and 1 tsp cumin. Simmer for 25 minutes until lentils are soft. Blend if desired. Season and serve with wholemeal bread. Freezes perfectly.

Budget Tips

  • Frozen vegetables — Just as nutritious as fresh, pre-chopped and much cheaper. Frozen berries, spinach and mixed veg are staples
  • Tinned fish — Sardines, mackerel and salmon provide excellent omega-3s at a fraction of fresh fish prices
  • Dried and tinned legumes — Lentils, chickpeas and beans are cheap, nutritious and anti-inflammatory
  • Seasonal produce — Buy what's in season for better prices and fresher flavour
  • Supermarket own brands — Often identical quality to named brands at lower cost
  • Cook once, eat twice — Double batch recipes and freeze portions

Kitchen Adaptations for Arthritis

  • Use pre-chopped frozen vegetables to avoid chopping
  • A food processor handles heavy chopping tasks
  • Electric tin opener eliminates painful twisting
  • Lightweight pans reduce wrist strain
  • Sit on a perching stool at the counter if standing is painful
  • Use a kettle tipper or lightweight cordless kettle

Meal planning takes the daily decision-making stress out of eating well with arthritis. Even following these plans loosely will increase your intake of anti-inflammatory foods. Our virtual assistant can suggest more recipes based on your dietary preferences.
